items.answer: Article 5(1)(a) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective, or the effect, of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or a group of persons [3]. Recital (29) explains that such systems deploy subliminal components such as audio, image or video stimuli that persons cannot perceive, or other manipulative or deceptive techniques that subvert or impair a person's autonomy, decision-making or free choice in ways people are not consciously aware of, or cannot control or resist even when aware [1]. The prohibition covers systems that cause or are reasonably likely to cause significant harm, including harms accumulated over time, and it is not necessary for the provider or deployer to intend the significant harm if it results from the manipulative or exploitative practices; intention to distort may not be assumed where distortion results from factors outside the control of the provider or deployer that are not reasonably foreseeable [2]. Recital (29) also notes that AI systems exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation are addressed [1][2]. The excerpts do not contain the full text of Article 5(1)(b)-(h) or any exceptions beyond the note that the prohibitions should not affect lawful practices in medical treatment such as psychological treatment of a mental disease [2], so the complete list of exceptions is not covered.

The excerpts do not contain the operative rule on social scoring. Recital (31) in excerpt [1] says AI systems providing social scoring of natural persons by public or private actors may lead to discriminatory outcomes and exclusion, may violate dignity and non-discrimination, and that the resulting social score may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. The excerpt cuts off before that sentence finishes. Whether a government may do this is decided by the prohibition in Article 5 (the excerpts do not include Article 5 or its wording), so the excerpts cannot confirm whether such ranking and penalising is banned, and under what conditions. The full text of Article 5 and its related recitals is needed.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts confirm whether government social scoring and penalising low scorers is banned.

items.answer: Partly. Recital (44) states that the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems intended to detect the emotional state of individuals in situations related to the workplace and education should be prohibited [1]. The recital says this prohibition should not cover AI systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, such as systems intended for therapeutical use [1]. Recital (17)-(19) defines an 'emotion recognition system' as an AI system for identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data, covering emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger and embarrassment, and excluding physical states such as pain or fatigue, and the mere detection of readily apparent expressions unless used to infer emotions [4]. Recital (44) also notes that the imbalance of power in work contexts makes such systems risky [1]. Where emotion recognition is used by a deployer, Article 50(3) requires the deployer to inform the natural persons exposed to it and to process personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable, subject to the law-enforcement exception stated there [2]. The excerpts do not include the text of the prohibition article itself (Article 5), its exact scope, or its exceptions, so I cannot confirm the full legal position from them. This is general information, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not include the text of the prohibition article (Article 5), its exact scope, or its exceptions.
contradicted_points: Answer's headline 'Partly' conflicts with the prohibition being general, though it notes the exception and that Article 5 text was not provided

items.answer: No. Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage [2]. Recital (43) explains the prohibition is because this practice adds to the feeling of mass surveillance and can lead to gross violations of fundamental rights, including the right to privacy [1]. The excerpts do not contain any exceptions to this specific prohibition, so the answer is based solely on the text provided.

Generally prohibited, with narrow exceptions. Article 5(1)(h) prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, unless and in so far as it is strictly necessary for one of three objectives: (i) targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and for missing persons; (ii) prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; (iii) localisation or identification of a suspected perpetrator of an Annex II offence punishable in the Member State by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years [4]. The objectives are described as exhaustively listed and narrowly defined, and their use must be strictly necessary to achieve a substantial public interest that outweighs the risks [2][4]. Use must be limited to confirming the specifically targeted individual's identity and to what is strictly necessary regarding time, geographic and personal scope [1]. It is authorised only if the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment and, unless provided otherwise, registered the system in the database [1]. Each use requires an express and specific authorisation by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority [1]. Article 5(2) adds further conditions (deployment for the purposes listed, with the rest of Article 5(2) not included in the excerpts). Excerpts do not include the full text of Article 5(2)-(6), the Annex II list, or the exact authorisation procedure and Member State derogation rules, so those details cannot be confirmed here. This is general information, not legal advice.

Partly. Recital (30) states that biometric categorisation systems based on natural persons' biometric data (such as face or fingerprint) to deduce or infer political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, race, sex life or sexual orientation should be prohibited [1]. The recital also says that prohibition should not cover the lawful labelling, filtering or categorisation of biometric data sets acquired in line with Union or national law, such as sorting images by hair or eye colour, which can for example be used in law enforcement [1]. Recital (15)-(17) explains that biometric categorisation means assigning natural persons to specific categories on the basis of their biometric data, and excludes systems that are a purely ancillary feature intrinsically linked to another commercial service [2]. The excerpts only show this as recital wording; they do not contain the operative prohibition text of Article 5, so the binding prohibition and its exact scope should be confirmed against Article 5 itself, which is not in the excerpts. Recital (39)-(40) also notes that for non-law-enforcement purposes, processing of biometric data is generally prohibited by Article 9(1) GDPR and Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 subject to limited exceptions [3]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The operative prohibition text of Article 5 is not contained in the excerpts and should be confirmed against Article 5.

items.answer: No, not where it is based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics. Article 5(1) prohibits putting into service or using an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, based solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics [2]. The prohibition does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of a person's involvement in a criminal activity, which is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity [2]. Recital (42)-(44) explains that the prohibition does not touch risk analytics not based on profiling of individuals or on their personality traits and characteristics, such as analytics of suspicious transactions or known trafficking routes [1]. Recital (59) also notes that, insofar as not prohibited, assessing the risk of reoffending is classed as high-risk when not solely based on profiling or personality traits [6]. The excerpts do not include the full text of the prohibition's wording beyond these points, so the answer is limited to the excerpted provisions. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

The excerpts do not contain the operative prohibition text (Article 5(1)(b)), but the recitals indicate that AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities are to be prohibited where they distort behaviour causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Recital (29) states that AI systems may exploit the vulnerabilities of a person or specific group due to their age or disability within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2019/882, or a specific social or economic situation, and that such AI systems 'should therefore be prohibited' when used with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm [1][2]. Harm need not be intended: it is not necessary for the provider or deployer to have the intention to cause significant harm, provided such harm results from the manipulative or exploitative AI-enabled practices [2]. Recital (29) also notes that the prohibitions do not affect lawful practices in medical treatment, such as psychological treatment of a mental disease [2]. The excerpts do not include the article text itself, so the exact legal wording, scope and any further exceptions should be checked against Article 5 of the Regulation. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Under Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement may be used to localise or identify a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, but only for offences referred to in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years [2]. Recital (33) explains that the Annex II list is based on the 32 offences in Council Framework Decision 2002/584/JHA, and that the four-year threshold is intended to ensure the offence is serious enough to potentially justify such use [3]. The use must also be strictly necessary and is subject to the safeguards in Article 5(2)-(3), including a fundamental rights impact assessment and authorisation [4]. Under Article 5(5) and Recital (38), a Member State may decide not to provide for this possibility at all, or to provide for it only for some objectives or some of the offences in point (h)(iii) [6][5]. The excerpts do not themselves list the individual Annex II offences, so the specific crimes are not identified here.

Article 3(1) defines an 'AI system' as a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments [1]. Recital (12) explains that the capacity to infer goes beyond basic data processing by enabling learning, reasoning or modelling, that 'machine-based' means the system runs on machines, and that adaptiveness refers to self-learning capabilities allowing the system to change while in use [4]. The excerpts do not include the full text of the definitions of the other terms in Article 3, so this answer is limited to the definition of AI system as quoted.
contexts: Annex III, point 8 – Annex IV, point 1

items.answer: Under Article 3(4), a 'deployer' is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity [6]. So the category covers any such person or body that uses an AI system under its authority, whether public or private, and the excerpts do not elaborate further on edge cases beyond that personal non-professional exclusion. Separately, the excerpts show that deployers of high-risk AI systems have obligations such as monitoring operation and informing providers and authorities (Article 26(5)) [1], and that some deployers (bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers under Annex III points 5(b) and (c)) must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27(1)) [4][5]. These later obligations apply only to the specific categories described in those provisions.

The excerpts do not contain the formal Article 3(63) definition itself, but they describe it. A general-purpose AI model is defined and set apart from AI systems based on its key functional characteristics: generality and the capability to competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks. Such models are typically trained on large amounts of data using methods such as self-supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning, and may be placed on the market via libraries, APIs, direct download or physical copy [1]. Models with at least a billion parameters, trained on large amounts of data using self-supervision at scale, should be considered to display significant generality [2]. Large generative AI models are a typical example [2]. Although AI models are essential components of AI systems, they do not constitute AI systems on their own, since they require further components such as a user interface [1]. A general-purpose AI model is distinct from a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, which is a model meeting the classification conditions in Article 51(1), including high-impact capabilities, presumed where cumulative training computation exceeds 10^25 floating point operations under Article 51(2) [5]. Note: the excerpts describe rather than quote the legal definition, so the exact wording of the definition should be checked in the official text.

Under Article 3(60), a 'deep fake' means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful [1]. Recital (134) uses similar wording, describing content that appreciably resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear authentic or truthful (deep fakes) [2]. Under Article 50(4), deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates deep fake content must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated [4]. Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, the disclosure is limited to revealing the existence of such content in a manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work [4]. The excerpts do not cover the Article 50(4) exception for use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences beyond noting it exists [4][6]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Generally no, with qualifications. Article 2(3) provides that the Regulation does not apply to AI systems where and in so far as they are placed on the market, put into service, or used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities [3]. It also does not apply to AI systems not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for such purposes [3]. Recital (24) explains that the exclusion does not prevent use for these purposes and that the regulation of AI in military and defence contexts falls under public international law [2][4]. The exclusion is limited to exclusive use: if a system developed or used for military, defence or national security purposes is used outside those purposes, for example civilian, humanitarian, law enforcement or public security purposes, it falls within the scope and the entity using it for other purposes should ensure compliance, unless already compliant [4]. Systems placed on the market for both excluded and non-excluded purposes fall within scope, and their providers must ensure compliance [4]. Note that the excerpts do not include the full text of Article 2(3) in its entirety, so this answer relies on the parts retrieved; it is not legal advice.

The excerpts only partly address this. In the recitals on general-purpose AI model obligations, the Regulation states that compliance should be proportionate and excludes the need for compliance for persons who develop or use models for non-professional or scientific research purposes, though they should be encouraged to comply voluntarily [6]. That concerns general-purpose AI models, not AI systems used for personal hobbies, and the excerpts do not include the Regulation's scope provisions, so they do not establish whether personal, non-professional use of an AI tool is outside the Act. This is information about the law, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts include the Regulation's scope provisions that determine whether personal, non-professional use of an AI tool is outside the Act.

items.answer: No, AI systems and models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development are excluded from the scope of the Regulation [1][5]. Article 2(8) states the Regulation does not apply to research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, that such activities must follow applicable Union law, and that testing in real world conditions is not covered by that exclusion [2]. Recital 25 adds that any other AI system that may be used for research and development remains subject to the Regulation, and that any research and development should follow recognised ethical and professional standards and applicable Union law [5]. The exclusion does not override the obligation to comply with the Regulation where an AI system within its scope is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such activity [1]. The excerpts do not give the full text of Article 2(6) or further detail on the sole-purpose wording beyond these points.

Partly. The excerpts indicate that the Regulation's scope extends to providers established in third countries: its rules apply to providers of AI systems in a non-discriminatory manner, irrespective of whether they are established within the Union or in a third country, and certain AI systems fall within scope even when not placed on the market, put into service, or used in the Union, for example where an EU-established operator contracts services to a third-country operator [3]. Recital 3 also refers to AI systems that can easily circulate across borders [6]. However, the excerpts do not contain the operative scope provision (Article 2(1)) that spells out when a non-EU provider is covered by reference to output used in the Union, so the precise conditions cannot be confirmed from these excerpts. Article 2(3) excludes systems not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where output is used in the Union exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes [5], which is a narrow carve-out. The excerpts also do not address whether a US company's specific system falls within the Regulation; that requires checking Article 2(1) and the definitions in full text. This is information about the law, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The AI Act definitively applies to a US company whose AI system output is used in the EU.

items.answer: The excerpts do not contain the AI literacy obligation itself (normally Article 4 of the Regulation). They only include Recital 20-22 and Recital 165, which say that AI literacy measures should be widely implemented and that the Board should support promotion of AI literacy tools and public awareness [1], that the Commission and Member States should facilitate voluntary codes of conduct to advance AI literacy among persons dealing with AI development, operation and use [1], and that providers and deployers should be encouraged to apply AI literacy measures on a voluntary basis [5]. The operative requirement and its article are not in the excerpts, so the mandatory scope cannot be stated from them.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts contain the operative mandatory AI literacy obligation (Article 4).

items.answer: The excerpts only partly answer this. An AI system is high-risk where it presents a high risk of harm to the health and safety or fundamental rights of persons, taking into account both the severity of the possible harm and its probability of occurrence, and it is used in pre-defined areas specified in the Regulation [5]. A system in those areas may not be high-risk where it does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making, which can occur where, for example, it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task [5]. Recital 61 states that AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and applying the law to a concrete set of facts are high-risk, and that alternative dispute resolution systems are high-risk where their outcomes produce legal effects for the parties. Purely ancillary administrative activities that do not affect the actual administration of justice in individual cases are not classified as high-risk [1]. Article 6(3) is referenced as the basis on which a provider may classify a system as non-high-risk, and a market surveillance authority may evaluate that classification against the Article 6(3) conditions and Commission guidelines [4]. Not covered by the excerpts: the Article 6 classification rules and conditions in full, the Annex III list of pre-defined high-risk areas, and the Article 6(3) conditions themselves. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Yes, but only under a narrow derogation. Article 6(3) provides that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making [2]. The derogation applies where at least one of the listed conditions is fulfilled: (a) the system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) it is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) it is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the Annex III use cases [2][4]. Recital 53 explains that these conditions reflect tasks of narrow and limited nature posing only limited risks [4]. Exception: an Annex III system is always considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons [1]. A provider who considers an Annex III system not high-risk must document its assessment before placing it on the market or putting it into service, must register under Article 49(2), and must provide the documentation to national competent authorities on request [1][5]. Market surveillance authorities may evaluate such a classification and require the provider to bring the system into compliance if it is found high-risk [6]. The excerpts do not set out the full list of Article 6(3) documentation details or the Commission guidelines referred to in Article 6(5).

Yes. Recital (57) states that AI systems used in employment, workers management and access to self-employment, in particular for the recruitment and selection of persons, should be classified as high-risk, since they may have an appreciable impact on future career prospects, livelihoods and workers' rights [5]. Recital (57) also notes that such systems may perpetuate historical patterns of discrimination throughout the recruitment process [5]. The excerpts do not include the operative text of the high-risk employment category (Annex III), so the precise legal wording and any conditions or exceptions for this category are not confirmed here. The recitals also state that AI systems intended only for a preparatory task, such as file handling (indexing, searching, text processing), may fall outside high-risk classification under certain conditions, but that exception does not apply where the system implies profiling [4]. Whether a specific CV-screening tool meets those conditions cannot be determined from these excerpts alone; the relevant Annex III employment provisions and Article 6 should be checked.

The excerpts do not state whether AI credit scoring systems are high-risk, and they do not include the Annex III provision on creditworthiness assessment that would decide this. They say only that AI systems used for detecting fraud in financial services and for prudential capital calculations of credit institutions and insurers should not be considered high-risk [2]. They also say that risk assessment and pricing for natural persons in health and life insurance can significantly affect livelihoods and lead to financial exclusion and discrimination [2], but they do not classify that as high-risk and do not address credit scoring. Confirming the answer requires the text of Annex III and Article 6 of the Regulation.
unsupported_claims: AI systems for risk assessment and pricing for health and life insurance are classified as high-risk.
contradicted_points: Yes, AI credit scoring systems are high-risk under the EU AI Act.

items.answer: Yes, in the regulation's own framing. Recital (57) states that AI systems used in education or vocational training, including for 'monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests', should be classified as high-risk AI systems, because they may determine a person's educational and professional course of life [1]. The excerpts do not include the operative Annex III wording or Article 6 text, so the precise legal classification mechanism is not confirmed here; the recital supports the classification as high-risk but the exact annex point and any exceptions are not covered by the excerpts provided.
unsupported_claims: The precise legal classification mechanism is confirmed by the excerpts.

items.answer: The excerpts state that AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons for health and life insurance can have a significant impact on persons' livelihood and, if not duly designed, developed and used, can infringe fundamental rights and lead to serious consequences such as financial exclusion and discrimination [1]. Recital (58) also says AI systems used to evaluate creditworthiness of natural persons are high-risk because they determine access to financial resources or essential services [4]. Recital (58) further states that AI systems used for detecting fraud in offering financial services and for prudential purposes to calculate credit institutions' and insurance undertakings' capital requirements should not be considered high-risk [1]. The excerpts do not include the operative Annex III point or Article 6 text that formally lists these uses, so the binding classification rule and any exceptions beyond these recitals are not confirmed here.

Under Annex III, point 7 (Migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law) [2], high-risk AI systems include: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies as polygraphs or similar tools [2]; (b) AI systems used by or on behalf of such authorities or Union bodies to assess a risk, including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or who has entered the territory of a Member State [2]; (c) AI systems used to assist competent public authorities in examining applications for asylum, visa or residence permits and associated complaints regarding the eligibility of natural persons, including related assessments of the reliability of evidence [2][4]; and (d) AI systems used in the context of migration, asylum or border control management for detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons, with the exception of the verification of travel documents [2][4]. Recital (60) explains these are classified as high-risk insofar as their use is permitted under relevant Union and national law [1][4]. Such systems must also be registered in a secure non-public section of the EU database under Article 49(4) [5]. The excerpts do not set out the full substantive requirements that apply to these systems.
citations: Annex III, point 6 – Annex III, point 8
contexts: Annex III, point 6 – Annex III, point 8

items.answer: Partly. Article 6(6) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of Article 6 by adding new conditions to those laid down there or modifying them, where there is concrete and reliable evidence of AI systems that fall under Annex III but do not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights [1]. Article 6(7) provides that the Commission shall adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to amend paragraph 3 [1]. Recital (174) states that the Commission should assess the need to amend the list of high-risk AI systems and the list of prohibited practices once a year [3]. The excerpts do not contain the full text of Article 7, which governs amendments to Annex III, so they do not confirm the exact procedure or conditions for adding new use cases to Annex III itself, and I cannot confirm that power from them.

Partly. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk where it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and the product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service under that legislation [2]. Recital (49) lists machinery and medical devices among such products and says that a product whose AI safety component undergoes third-party conformity assessment under the relevant harmonisation legislation is classified as high-risk [1]. Article 3 defines a safety component as a component that fulfils a safety function for a product or AI system, or whose failure or malfunctioning endangers the health and safety of persons or property [5]. Recital (49) adds that classifying the AI system as high-risk does not necessarily mean the product itself is high-risk under the criteria of the sector legislation, and cites Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746 as examples [1]. The excerpts do not include the text of Annex I or the sector legislation, so they do not confirm the specific conformity assessment requirements that apply to particular machinery or medical devices; that must be checked against Annex I and the applicable legislation. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Under Article 9(2), the risk management system must be a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating [2]. It must be established, implemented, documented and maintained [2]. It comprises the following steps: (a) identification and analysis of the known and reasonably foreseeable risks the system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when used in accordance with its intended purpose; (b) estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the system is used in accordance with its intended purpose and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse [2]. Recital (65) adds that providers should identify risks or adverse impacts, implement mitigation measures for known and reasonably foreseeable risks, consider reasonably foreseeable misuse and the interaction with the environment, document and explain the choices made for risk-management measures, and include relevant known or foreseeable circumstances in the instructions for use [5]. Article 9(6)-(8) adds that high-risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds, at any time during development and in any event before being placed on the market or put into service [1]. Article 9(9) requires providers to consider whether the system is likely to adversely impact persons under 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups [1]. The excerpts do not contain the remaining steps of Article 9(2) (points (c) onward) or the full text of Article 9(3)-(5), so those requirements are not covered here.
unsupported_claims: Article 9(2)(b) requires estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the system is used in accordance with its intended purpose and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse.

items.answer: Under Article 10(3), training, validation and testing data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose [3]. They must have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used; these characteristics may be met at the level of individual data sets or a combination thereof [3]. Under Article 10(4), data sets must take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting in which the system is intended to be used [3]. Recital (65)-(67) states the same aims: data sets should be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete, requiring appropriate data governance and management practices [1]. Article 42(1) provides a presumption of compliance with Article 10(4) for systems trained and tested on data reflecting the specific setting of intended use [4]. Article 10(5) allows exceptional processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction only where strictly necessary and subject to appropriate safeguards and further conditions [3]; the excerpts do not contain the full list of those conditions.

Yes, but only exceptionally. Article 10(5) allows providers of high-risk AI systems to process special categories of personal data, which include ethnicity-related data, to the extent that it is strictly necessary for ensuring bias detection and correction in relation to those systems, subject to appropriate safeguards for the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons [4]. Recital (69) describes this as exceptional and as a matter of substantial public interest within the meaning of Article 9(2)(g) GDPR and Article 10(2)(g) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 [1]. The processing is in addition to, not instead of, Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680 [4][1]. Article 10(5) also requires that all the following conditions be met, and the excerpt is cut off before listing them in full; it begins with the condition that bias detection and correction cannot be effectively achieved by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data [4]. The remaining conditions are not included in the excerpts, so they cannot be fully stated here. The excerpts also show that bias in training data is a recognised concern that providers must address, with data sets required to be relevant, sufficiently representative and free of errors as far as possible [3][4]. Consult Article 10(5) in full for the complete list of conditions.
unsupported_claims: Special categories of personal data include ethnicity-related data.
One condition is that bias detection and correction cannot be effectively achieved by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data.

items.answer: The excerpts only partly answer this. Recital (71) says technical documentation should contain information needed to assess the system's compliance and facilitate post-market monitoring, including the system's general characteristics, capabilities and limitations, algorithms, data, training, testing and validation processes, and documentation on the risk-management system, presented in a clear and comprehensive form [1]. It should be kept up to date throughout the system's lifetime [1]. The excerpts do not contain the operative requirements on technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV, which Article 16(d) refers to via Article 18), so the binding list of required contents is not covered here [5]. Recitals are interpretive, so check Article 11 and Annex IV for the binding content [1][5]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Yes. Article 12(1) requires that high-risk AI systems technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system [1]. Recital (72) states the same principle, that high-risk AI systems should technically allow for the automatic recording of events, by means of logs, over the duration of the lifetime of the system [2]. The logging capabilities must enable recording of events relevant for identifying risk situations or substantial modifications, facilitating post-market monitoring under Article 72, and monitoring operation under Article 26(5) [1]. For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, Article 12(3) sets minimum content: start and end date and time of each use, the reference database checked, the input data matching, and identification of the natural persons involved in verifying results [1]. Providers must keep the automatically generated logs, to the extent under their control, for at least six months unless other Union or national law provides otherwise [3], and deployers have a similar six-month retention duty under Article 26(6) [6]. The excerpts do not set out the full scope of Article 12 beyond these points.

Under Article 13(2)-(3), high-risk AI systems must be accompanied by instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise, containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers [1]. The instructions must contain at least: (a) the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative; and (b) the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the system, including its intended purpose; the level of accuracy, including metrics, robustness and cybersecurity against which it was tested and validated, and any known and foreseeable circumstances affecting that expected level [1]; any known or foreseeable circumstance related to use in line with its intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights [1]; where applicable, technical capabilities and characteristics to provide information relevant to explain its output [1]; and, when appropriate, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which it is intended to be used [1]. The excerpt is cut off at item (vi), so the remaining items of Article 13(3) are not covered. Recital (72) adds that instructions should include illustrative examples on limitations and intended and precluded uses where appropriate, and should be in a language easily understood by target deployers as determined by the Member State [5].

Under Article 14, human oversight must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use of the high-risk AI system, and ensured through one or both of: (a) measures identified and built, when technically feasible, into the system by the provider before it is placed on the market or put into service; or (b) measures identified by the provider that are appropriate for the deployer to implement [1]. The system must be provided to the deployer so that the natural persons assigned oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to properly understand the system's capacities and limitations and monitor its operation, including detecting anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; to remain aware of automation bias, particularly where outputs are used for recommendations to decisions; and to correctly interpret the output [1]. Article 14(2) states that oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when the system is used in accordance with its intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable misuse, especially where such risks persist despite other requirements [1]. Article 14(1) and Article 13(3) add that the system must be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so it can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use, and that providers must give deployers information such as the human oversight measures and technical measures facilitating interpretation of outputs [2]. The excerpts do not cover the full text of Article 14(5) or other detailed requirements for specific systems.

High-risk AI systems must achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity in light of their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art, and perform consistently throughout their lifecycle [3]. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics must be declared in the accompanying instructions of use [4][5]; the Commission is to encourage development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies with stakeholders [4]. Robustness: they must be as resilient as possible against errors, faults or inconsistencies in the system or its environment, with technical and organisational measures required; redundancy solutions such as backup or fail-safe plans may achieve this; and systems that keep learning after market placement must address feedback loops with mitigation measures (Article 15(4)) [4]. Recitals describe fail-safe mechanisms that can safely interrupt operation when anomalies arise or operation falls outside predetermined boundaries [1]. Cybersecurity: they must be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities, with technical solutions appropriate to the circumstances and risks, including measures to prevent, detect, respond to and resolve AI-specific vulnerabilities such as data poisoning and adversarial attacks (Article 15(5)) [4][1]. Under Recital (77)-(78), high-risk AI systems within scope of the horizontal cybersecurity regulation for products with digital elements may demonstrate compliance with the cybersecurity requirements by fulfilling its essential cybersecurity requirements, as shown in the EU declaration of conformity [2]. Instructions for use must state the accuracy level and metrics, and robustness and cybersecurity levels tested against, under Article 13(3)(b)(ii) [5]. The excerpts do not give the full text of the remaining Article 15 provisions or any specific numerical accuracy thresholds.

Providers of high-risk AI systems must: ensure compliance with the Section 2 requirements [2]; indicate their name, registered trade name or trade mark and contact address on the system, its packaging or accompanying documentation [2]; have a quality management system complying with Article 17 [2]; keep the documentation referred to in Article 18 [2]; keep automatically generated logs under their control as referred to in Article 19 [2]; ensure the system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment under Article 43 before being placed on the market or put into service [2]; draw up an EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 [2]; affix the CE marking under Article 48 [2]; comply with registration obligations under Article 49(1) [2]; and take necessary corrective actions and provide information as required by Article 20 [2]. Under Article 20(2), if they consider a system non-compliant or a risk exists, they must immediately investigate causes, inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body, and describe the non-compliance and corrective action taken [6]. On reasoned request by a competent authority, they must provide information and documentation demonstrating conformity, in an easily understood official Union language, and give access to logs under their control [6]. Providers established in third countries must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate before making such systems available on the Union market [6]. Providers must also ensure outputs of generative systems are marked machine-readable and detectable as artificially generated, under Article 50(2) [1]. The excerpts also describe a risk management system as a continuous iterative process throughout the lifecycle (Article 9(1)-(2)) [3], and testing before placing on the market (Article 9(6)-(8)) [5]; the excerpts do not fully cover all Article 16 and Article 17 to 19 details, which are only referenced here.

The excerpts only partly answer this. Annex VII point 2 says the application to a notified body must include a description of the quality management system, which shall cover all the aspects listed under Article 17 [2]. Annex VI point 1 says the provider verifies that the established quality management system complies with the requirements of Article 17 [4]. The excerpts do not reproduce the full list of Article 17 aspects, so I cannot enumerate them. Other points the excerpts do show: the provider must describe procedures ensuring the system remains adequate and effective [2], and must keep it implemented and maintained so it remains adequate and efficient [2]. Any intended change must be brought to the notified body's attention [2]. Providers must keep documentation concerning the quality management system referred to in Article 17 for 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service [3]. Providers that are financial institutions may treat the obligation as fulfilled by complying with internal governance rules under Union financial services law, with the exception of Article 17(1)(g), (h) and (i) [3]. Recital 81 notes that providers subject to sectoral quality management obligations may include the Regulation's elements within that existing system [1]. The full content of Article 17 is needed to answer completely.

The excerpts do not state how long a provider must keep the technical documentation under Article 18. Excerpt [2] only says that financial institutions keep technical documentation as part of their documentation under Union financial services law, and excerpt [4] refers to keeping the Article 18 documentation without a period. The excerpts do give a minimum of at least six months for logs (Article 19(1), excerpt [2]), but that is a different obligation and should not be taken as the documentation retention period. The Article 18 text itself is needed to answer this.

Providers must keep the automatically generated logs, to the extent under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise, in particular Union data protection law [2][6]. Deployers have the same obligation for logs under their control, for at least six months unless otherwise provided by Union or national law, in particular Union data protection law [3]. Providers and deployers that are financial institutions subject to Union financial services law instead maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept under that financial services law [2][3]. The excerpts do not state a maximum retention period.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems have several obligations drawn from the excerpts. They must use the systems in accordance with the instructions for use and take appropriate technical and organisational measures to do so [6]. They must ensure that persons assigned human oversight have the necessary competence, including an adequate level of AI literacy, training and authority [6]; human oversight measures must be commensurate with risks, autonomy and context of use, and be built in by the provider or be appropriate for the deployer to implement [5]. To the extent they control input data, they must ensure it is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose (Article 26(4)) [1]. They must monitor operation based on the instructions for use and inform providers where relevant (Article 26(5)) [1]. Where they have reason to consider use may present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), they must without undue delay inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority and suspend use; where they identify a serious incident, they must immediately inform first the provider, then the importer or distributor and the market surveillance authorities (Article 26(5)) [1]. They must cooperate with competent authorities in any action taken regarding the system (Article 26(12)) [2]. Deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, and deployers of systems under points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III must, before deployment, perform a fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27(1)) [2]. Where systems make or assist decisions about natural persons, deployers must inform those persons that they are subject to the system (Article 26(11)) [2]. Record-keeping and monitoring obligations are also referred to in general terms [6]. Exceptions noted: the serious incident reporting obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of law enforcement deployers, and financial institutions subject to Union financial services governance rules have a modified monitoring obligation [1]. The excerpts do not fully set out the record-keeping details or the full text of the monitoring obligation for financial institutions, so those parts are not covered. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

The excerpts do not contain the specific deployer obligation to inform workers. Recital (92) states that the Regulation is without prejudice to employers' obligations to inform or to inform and consult workers or their representatives under Union or national law and practice, including Directive 2002/14/EC, on decisions to put into service or use AI systems, and that it remains necessary to ensure information of workers and their representatives on the planned deployment of high-risk AI systems at the workplace [4]. However, the excerpts do not state the exact content, timing or form of that information duty, nor which deployer article sets it out, so the precise requirement under the Regulation and Directive 2002/14/EC (and any national law) cannot be confirmed from them. The excerpts also do not cover Article 26 deployer obligations in full. Please consult the full text of the Regulation, Directive 2002/14/EC and applicable national law.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, and deployers of certain high-risk AI systems listed in an annex, such as banking or insurance entities, must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to putting the system into use [1][5]. Article 27(1) states this applies to high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2), with the exception of systems intended for the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, and to deployers of systems referred to in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III [5]. The assessment must cover the deployer's processes, the period and frequency of use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, and the specific risks of harm [5]. The excerpts do not include the full text of Article 27, so further paragraphs and any additional conditions are not covered.

Under Article 22(1), before making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market, providers established in third countries must, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union [4]. The excerpts do not show the rest of Article 22 (such as the mandate's contents or the representative's further duties), so those details are not covered here. The excerpts also do not contain the separate registration duties of providers, which are in Article 49(1) [1].
unsupported_claims: Providers outside the EU must register their high-risk AI systems in the EU database under Article 49(1).

items.answer: Under Article 23(1), before placing a high-risk AI system on the market an importer must verify that: (a) the provider has undergone the relevant conformity assessment procedure [1]; (b) the provider has drawn up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV [1]; (c) the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and instructions for use [1]; and (d) the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1) [1]. Under Article 23(2), if the importer has sufficient reason to consider that the system is not in conformity with the Regulation, is falsified, or is accompanied by falsified documentation, it must not place the system on the market until it has been brought into conformity; if the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the importer must inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities [1]. Note: the excerpt for point (a) is truncated, so the exact wording of that conformity assessment requirement is not fully shown in the excerpts provided.
unsupported_claims: Under Article 23(1), an importer must verify that the provider has undergone the relevant conformity assessment procedure before placing a high-risk AI system on the market.

items.answer: Yes, under Article 25(1)(b), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is considered a provider of a high-risk AI system, and subject to the Article 16 provider obligations, if they make a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that has already been placed on the market or put into service in such a way that it remains a high-risk AI system pursuant to Article 6 [1]. In that case, under Article 25(2), the original provider no longer counts as the provider of that system [1]. The excerpts do not state the full definition of 'substantial modification', so the exact threshold is not covered. Article 25(2) also requires the initial provider to closely cooperate with the new provider and provide the reasonably expected technical access, information and assistance, unless it has clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk AI system [5][2]. Article 25(1)(a) (putting your name or trademark on the system) and 25(1)(c) (modifying intended purpose) are separate triggers not asked about here [1].

Under Article 24, distributors of high-risk AI systems must: (1) verify, before making a system available, that it bears the required CE marking and has the required documentation and instructions, which the excerpts do not show in full, so this is only partly covered; (2) where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), inform the provider or importer, and immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities, giving details of the non-compliance and corrective actions taken [1]; (3) ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with Section 2 requirements [1]; (4) if they consider or have reason to consider a system they have made available is not in conformity with Section 2, take the corrective actions necessary to bring it into conformity, withdraw or recall it, or ensure the provider, importer or other relevant operator does so [1]; (5) upon a reasoned request from a competent authority, provide all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity with Section 2 [1]; (6) cooperate with relevant competent authorities in any action they take regarding such a system, in particular to reduce or mitigate the risk [2]. Under Article 25(1), a distributor becomes subject to provider obligations under Article 16 if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system already on the market, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose so that a non-high-risk system becomes high-risk, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating obligations otherwise [2]. Recital (85)-(88) adds that the former provider should still cooperate and provide necessary information and technical access in such cases [3]. The excerpts do not include the full text of Article 24(1) or (2), so the complete list of pre-market distributor checks is not covered.
unsupported_claims: Distributors must verify before making a system available that it bears the required CE marking and has required documentation and instructions.

items.answer: The excerpts show that Annex III high-risk AI systems follow different procedures depending on the point of Annex III. For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers must follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control in Annex VI, which does not involve a notified body [5]. For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), the provider, where it has applied harmonised standards under Article 40 or common specifications under Article 41, must choose either internal control (Annex VI) or the assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation with a notified body (Annex VII) [2]. Where harmonised standards or common specifications are absent, not applied, only partly applied, or restricted, Article 43(1) points (a) to (d) require the Annex VII procedure, and the provider may choose any notified body; for systems used by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or Union institutions, the market surveillance authority acts as notified body [5]. The excerpts do not cover the full text of Article 43 or the content of Annexes VI and VII beyond these references, and they do not address the separate rules for Annex III systems that the provider has documented as not high-risk under Article 6(3) [1][4].
unsupported_claims: Annex III point 1 covers biometrics.

items.answer: Yes, in the event of a substantial modification. Article 43(4) states that high-risk AI systems that have already been subject to a conformity assessment procedure shall undergo a new conformity assessment procedure in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is intended to be further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer [3]. The excerpts do not define "substantial modification". For high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service, changes that have been pre-determined by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment are addressed in the remainder of Article 43(4), which is cut off in the excerpt, so its conditions cannot be stated here [3]. Article 17(1)(a) also refers to a strategy covering procedures for the management of modifications to the high-risk AI system [5].
unsupported_claims: The excerpts define the term "substantial modification."

items.answer: Under Article 48(3), the CE marking must be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly for high-risk AI systems [1]. Where that is not possible or not warranted given the nature of the system, it must be affixed to the packaging or to the accompanying documentation, as appropriate [1]. Article 16(h) requires providers to affix the CE marking in this way, in accordance with Article 48, to indicate conformity with the Regulation [2]. Where applicable, the CE marking is followed by the identification number of the notified body responsible for the conformity assessment under Article 43, which is affixed by the body itself or, under its instructions, by the provider or its authorised representative [1]. Recital (129) adds that for high-risk AI systems embedded in a product a physical CE marking should be affixed, which may be complemented by a digital CE marking, and for systems only provided digitally a digital CE marking should be used [3]. The excerpts do not cover every detail of the marking's digital form or the full text of Article 48(1)-(2), so those points are not addressed here.
unsupported_claims: Recital (129) states that for high-risk AI systems embedded in a product a physical CE marking should be affixed, which may be complemented by a digital CE marking.

items.answer: The EU declaration of conformity must state that the high-risk AI system meets the Section 2 requirements and must contain the information set out in Annex V [1]. Annex V (as reflected in the excerpt of its contents) requires: (1) AI system name and type plus any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability [3]; (2) the name and address of the provider or, where applicable, its authorised representative [3]; (3) a statement that the declaration is issued under the sole responsibility of the provider [3]; (4) a statement that the AI system is in conformity with the Regulation and, if applicable, other relevant Union law providing for such a declaration [3]; (5) where personal data is processed, a statement of compliance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680 [3]; (6) references to any relevant harmonised standards or common specifications used [3]; (7) where applicable, the notified body's name and identification number, a description of the conformity assessment procedure performed, and identification of the certificate issued [3]; (8) the place and date of issue, the name and function of the signatory, an indication for whom the person signed, and a signature [3]. The declaration must be translated into a language easily understood by the national competent authorities where the system is placed on the market or made available [1]. Where other Union harmonisation legislation also requires a declaration, a single declaration may be drawn up covering all applicable Union law, containing the information needed to identify that legislation [1]. By drawing up the declaration, the provider assumes responsibility for compliance with Section 2 and must keep it up-to-date [1]. The Commission may amend Annex V by delegated act [1]. The excerpts do not cover the full content of Annex V beyond the points listed, nor the details of the conformity assessment procedures themselves.
citations: Annex IV, point 9 – Annex VI, point 1
contexts: Annex IV, point 9 – Annex VI, point 1

items.answer: Yes, in general. Article 49(1) of the Regulation requires providers of high-risk AI systems to register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before placing them on the market or putting them into service; this is also listed as a provider obligation in Article 16(i) [2][5]. Article 49(3) requires deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, or persons acting on their behalf, to register themselves, select the system and register its use before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, except for the systems in point 2 of Annex III [2]. Recital 131 says other deployers may register voluntarily [4]. For high-risk systems in law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III points 1, 6 and 7), registration is made in a secure non-public section of the database, with access strictly limited to the Commission and national authorities [1][2]. Under Article 49(5), high-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure) are registered at national level only [3]. The excerpts do not set out the full content of Article 71 or the detailed registration procedure.
unsupported_claims: Article 49(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

items.answer: Yes, in general. Recital (132) states that natural persons should be notified that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person taking into account the circumstances and context of use [2]. The excerpts do not include the operative text of Article 50(1) that sets this out as a legal obligation for providers, so the binding rule and its details (such as timing) are not confirmed here. Article 50(5) says the required information must be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements [5]. Article 50(6) notes these duties are without prejudice to other transparency obligations under Union or national law for deployers [5]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: Users must be told they are talking to a chatbot in all cases.

items.answer: Only in part. Providers must embed technical solutions that mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as AI-generated, as far as technically feasible; this marking obligation should not cover AI systems performing primarily an assistive function for standard editing or not substantially altering the input data or its semantics [1][3]. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Art. 50(4)) [3][4]. Deep fakes are content that appreciably resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear authentic [4]. The disclosure duty does not apply where use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences [3]. For evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, the duty is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated content in a way that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work [3][4]. For AI-generated text, deployers must disclose that it is artificially generated when it is published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless it has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for publication [3][5]. Disclosure must be clear and distinguishable, at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure [5]. The excerpts do not contain the full operative text of Art. 50(2) on providers' marking duty, nor any general labelling rule for all AI-generated text or images outside these cases, so those points cannot be confirmed from the excerpts.

Deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system must inform the natural persons exposed to it of the operation of the system [2] (Article 50(3)). Recital (132) explains that natural persons should be notified when they are exposed to AI systems that, by processing their biometric data, can identify or infer their emotions or intentions or assign them to specific categories, such as sex, age, hair colour, eye colour, tattoos, personal traits, ethnic origin, personal preferences and interests [6]. Such information should be provided in accessible formats for persons with disabilities [6]. Article 50(3) also requires that personal data be processed in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable [2]. The notice obligation does not apply to biometric categorisation and emotion recognition systems permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards and Union law [2]. The excerpts do not give the exact wording of the notice content or format beyond these points.
contexts: Annex III, point 1 – Annex III, point 4

items.answer: A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities, and therefore to be a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a), when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10^25 (Article 51(2)) [5]. This reflects the recital rationale that training computation is one of the relevant approximations for model capabilities, including computation across pre-training, synthetic data generation and fine-tuning [1]. The presumption is rebuttable in the sense that the provider may, when notifying, submit sufficiently substantiated arguments that, exceptionally, its model does not present systemic risks due to its specific characteristics (Article 52(2)); if the Commission finds those arguments insufficiently substantiated, it rejects them and the model is considered to have systemic risk (Article 52(3)) [4][2]. The provider must notify the Commission without delay and within two weeks after the requirement is met or it becomes known it will be met (Article 52(1)) [5][2]. Separately, the Commission may designate a model as presenting systemic risk ex officio or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel, based on Annex XIII criteria, and the Commission may amend the thresholds by delegated act (Articles 51(1)(b), 51(3), 52(4)) [5][4]. Note: the excerpts do not state the exact notification mechanics beyond those points, and the Article 52(1) text is partly truncated.

Under Article 52(4), the Commission may designate a general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risks, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel pursuant to Article 90(1), point (a), on the basis of the criteria set out in Annex XIII [2]. The excerpts also show the underlying classification basis: a model is classified as having systemic risk if it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks (Article 51(1), point (a)) [1]; or, under Article 51(1), point (b), if based on a Commission decision (ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel) it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to point (a), having regard to the criteria in Annex XIII [1]. Article 51(2) presumes high impact capabilities where the cumulative training compute is greater than 10^25 floating point operations [1]. Recital (111) explains that high-impact capabilities means capabilities that match or exceed those recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models, and that training compute is one of the relevant approximations for model capabilities [4]. Under Article 52(3), if the Commission rejects a provider's arguments that a model does not present systemic risks due to its specific characteristics, the model is considered to be a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk [2]. The excerpts do not set out the content of Annex XIII itself, so the specific criteria listed there are not covered.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts set out the specific content of the criteria listed in Annex XIII.

items.answer: Under Article 53(1), providers of general-purpose AI models must, among other things: (a) draw up and keep up to date technical documentation, including training and testing process and evaluation results, for provision to the AI Office and national competent authorities on request; (b) draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation for providers of AI systems that intend to integrate the model, so they understand its capabilities and limitations, containing at a minimum the elements in Annex XII, subject to Union and national law on business information and trade secrets [2]; (c) put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including identifying and complying with reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [2]; and (d) draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, according to a template provided by the AI Office [2]. Under Article 53(3), they must cooperate as necessary with the Commission and national competent authorities [2]. Recital (100) explains that proportionate transparency measures, including documentation, are meant to let downstream providers understand the model [1]. Recital (97) states that these obligations apply once the model is placed on the market [6]. Exception: under Article 53(2), points (a) and (b) do not apply to providers of models released under a free and open-source licence that allows access, usage, modification and distribution, whose parameters including weights, architecture and usage information are publicly available; this exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risks [2][3]. Article 53(4) allows providers to rely on codes of practice, though the excerpt is cut off before its details [2]. Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk have additional obligations under Article 55(1), including model evaluation with adversarial testing, assessing and mitigating systemic risks at Union level, reporting serious incidents without undue delay, and ensuring cybersecurity protection [3][5]. The excerpts do not contain the full text of Annex XII or the template, nor the complete Article 55 list beyond point (d).
unsupported_claims: Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up to date technical documentation, including training and testing process and evaluation results, for provision to the AI Office and national competent authorities on request.

items.answer: Partly. Providers of general-purpose AI models released under a free and open-source licence, whose parameters (including weights, architecture information and usage information) are made publicly available, are exempt from the transparency-related obligations in Article 53 (excerpt 4 and excerpt 1). This exemption does not apply where the model presents systemic risks; in that case the open-source licence is not a sufficient reason to exclude compliance [1][4]. The exemption also does not cover the obligation to produce a public summary of the content used for training and the obligation to have a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including identifying and complying with reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [1]. The excerpts do not set out the full list of obligations in Article 53 or any further conditions, so the precise scope of the exemption beyond these points cannot be confirmed from them.

In addition to the obligations in Articles 53 and 54, providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must under Article 55(1): (a) perform model evaluation under standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including documented adversarial testing, to identify and mitigate systemic risks [5]; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, that may stem from development, placing on the market, or use of the model [5]; (c) keep track of, document, and report without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities, relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures [5][1]; and (d) ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure, which may include securing model weights, algorithms, servers and data sets [5][1]. Recital (114) says these providers should assess and mitigate possible systemic risks [1]. A model is classified as one with systemic risk under Article 51(1) if it has high-impact capabilities (presumed where training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs under Article 51(2)) or equivalent capabilities or impact designated by the Commission [4]. Providers may argue exceptionally that their model does not present systemic risks under Article 52(2) [6]. The excerpts do not fully set out the content of Articles 53 and 54, so the baseline obligations are not described here. Article 54(6) states that the Article 54 obligation does not apply to certain free and open-source models unless they present systemic risks [5].

The provider must notify the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks after the high-impact capability requirement (Article 51(1), point (a)) is met or it becomes known that it will be met [2]. Recital (111) refers to notifying the AI Office at the latest two weeks after the requirements are met or become known to be met, and notes that a model exceeding the 10^25 floating point operations threshold is presumed to be a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk [1][2]. The excerpts do not state the exact notification content beyond information necessary to demonstrate the requirement has been met [2], and they do not cover the Commission's procedure after notification in full.

Codes of practice are a central tool for providers of general-purpose AI models to comply with their obligations under the Regulation, and providers can rely on them to demonstrate compliance [1]. They should cover obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models and of general-purpose AI models presenting systemic risks, help establish a risk taxonomy of systemic risks at Union level, and focus on specific risk assessment and mitigation measures [1]. Under Article 56(6), the AI Office and the Board assess whether the codes cover the obligations in Articles 53 and 55 and publish their assessment of adequacy, and the Commission may approve a code by implementing act and give it general validity within the Union [4][1]. Under Article 56(7), the AI Office may invite all general-purpose AI model providers to adhere; for providers not presenting systemic risks, adherence may be limited to Article 53 obligations unless they explicitly declare interest in the full code [4]. Codes are to address cybersecurity and serious incident reporting topics for systemic-risk models, and the AI Office should encourage and facilitate their drawing up, review and adaptation [2].
