Where a code cannot be finalised in time or is not deemed adequate by the AI Office, the Commission may instead provide common rules for implementing the relevant obligations [1]. Once a harmonised standard is published and assessed as suitable by the AI Office, compliance with it grants a presumption of conformity [1]. Not covered by the excerpts: the full text of Article 56(9) on the fallback date after 2 August 2025 and the content of the final codes.
unsupported_claims: Codes of practice are to address cybersecurity and serious incident reporting topics for systemic-risk models.

items.answer: AI regulatory sandboxes are controlled environments that foster innovation and facilitate the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before they are placed on the market or put into service, under a specific sandbox plan agreed between the providers or prospective providers and the competent authority [2]. Their objectives include establishing a controlled experimentation and testing environment in the development and pre-marketing phase to ensure compliance with the Regulation and other Union and national law, enhancing legal certainty for innovators, and facilitating regulatory learning [1]. Testing in real world conditions may be included, supervised within the sandbox [2][3]. Competent authorities provide guidance, supervision and support to identify risks, including to fundamental rights, health and safety [2]. Significant risks must result in adequate mitigation, and if no effective mitigation is possible, national competent authorities may suspend the testing or participation [6]. The excerpts state that national competent authorities establish the sandboxes (Article 57 and Recital 139 refer to 'national competent authorities establishing AI regulatory sandboxes') [3][2]; the excerpts do not contain the full text of Article 57(1) setting out the precise obligation on Member States to establish them, so the exact establishing obligation (e.g., deadlines or which Member States must act) is not covered here.
unsupported_claims: National competent authorities are the bodies that establish AI regulatory sandboxes.
The Article 57 and Recital 139 excerpts explicitly state that national competent authorities establish the sandboxes.

items.answer: Yes. Excerpt [4] states that providers or prospective providers may conduct testing of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III in real-world conditions at any time before placing on the market or putting into service, either on their own or in partnership with one or more deployers or prospective deployers (Article 60(2)). This is subject to conditions: testing may be conducted only where all of the listed conditions in Article 60(4) are met, including that the provider has drawn up a real-world testing plan and submitted it to the market surveillance authority in the Member State where testing is to be conducted (Article 60(4)(a)), and the excerpt is cut off before listing the remaining conditions, including point (b) about the market surveillance authority. The testing is without prejudice to the prohibitions under Article 5 and to any required ethical review (Article 60(1) and 60(3)) [4]. Article 9(7) also notes that testing procedures may include testing in real-world conditions in accordance with Article 60, and Article 9(8) states testing must be done before placing on the market or putting into service [1]. The excerpts do not contain the full list of Article 60(4) conditions, so those remaining requirements are not covered.

The excerpts describe several support measures. Priority access: Member States should give SMEs, including start-ups, with a registered office or branch in the Union priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes, provided they meet eligibility conditions and selection criteria, without precluding other providers from access on the same conditions [4]. Sandbox access is to be free of charge for SMEs and start-ups, without prejudice to exceptional costs that national competent authorities may recover in a fair and proportionate manner [5] (Article 58(2)(d)). Sandboxes must be open to any applying provider or prospective provider meeting transparent and fair criteria, with decisions communicated within three months [5] (Article 58(2)(a)). Conformity assessment fees: the specific interests and needs of SME providers, including start-ups, must be taken into account when setting fees under Article 43, reducing them proportionately to size, market size and other relevant indicators [2] (Article 63(2)); notified bodies should likewise consider these interests when setting fees [4]. Microenterprises may comply with certain elements of the quality management system under Article 17 in a simplified manner, provided they have no partner or linked enterprises [2] (Article 63(1)). Information and guidance: the AI Office is to provide standardised templates upon the Board's request, develop and maintain a single information platform, organise communication campaigns, and promote best practices in public procurement [2][1] (Article 62(1)(a)-(b) and Article 62(3)). Member States and the AI Office should use dedicated channels to communicate with SMEs, provide training tailored to their needs, and facilitate their participation in standardisation processes [2][4]. The Commission should regularly assess certification and compliance costs for SMEs and work with Member States to lower them, and Member States should consider language arrangements for documentation to reduce translation costs [4]. Medium-sized enterprises that until recently were small enterprises should also have access to these support measures [1]. The excerpts do not provide full details on the sandbox eligibility criteria, the content of the templates, or the precise scope of the simplified quality management obligations; those are not covered here.

The Board is composed of one representative per Member State [1]. The European Data Protection Supervisor participates as an observer, and the AI Office attends the Board's meetings without taking part in the votes [1]. Other national and Union authorities, bodies or experts may be invited on a case-by-case basis where the issues discussed are relevant to them [1]. Each representative is designated by their Member State for a period of three years, renewable once [1]. Member States must ensure their representatives have the relevant competences and powers in their Member State [1]. The Board is chaired by one of the Member State representatives, and the AI Office provides its secretariat [6]. The excerpts do not give the full text of the Member State representatives' competence requirements beyond the opening words of Article 65(4)(a), so those details are not covered.

The scientific panel is a panel of independent experts that the Commission establishes by implementing act to support enforcement under the Regulation [1][2]. Its members are selected by the Commission on the basis of up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in AI, and must have particular expertise and competence, be independent from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models, and be able to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively [1]. Its main role is to advise and support the AI Office, in particular on the implementation and enforcement of the Regulation as regards general-purpose AI models and systems [1][2]. It supports the AI Office's monitoring activities and may, where it has reason to suspect that a general-purpose AI model poses a concrete and identifiable risk at Union level, or meets the criteria for systemic risk classification, provide a reasoned qualified alert to the AI Office, which can trigger follow-up such as investigations [5][6]. Member States may also call upon its experts to support their own enforcement activities, possibly for fees [4]. The excerpts do not give the full list of the panel's tasks or the details of the implementing act, which are only partly covered here.

Each Member State must designate at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority as national competent authorities for supervising the application and implementation of the Regulation [1]. National competent authorities means a notifying authority or a market surveillance authority [5]. Each Member State should designate a market surveillance authority to act as a single point of contact [1]. Member States may appoint any kind of public entity to perform these tasks, according to their national organisational characteristics and needs [1]. For high-risk AI systems related to products under Annex I Section A, the market surveillance authority is the authority designated under those sectoral legal acts, though Member States may designate another relevant authority in appropriate circumstances, provided coordination with the sectoral authorities is ensured [6]. For high-risk AI systems placed on the market or used by financial institutions regulated by Union financial services law, the market surveillance authority is the relevant national financial supervisory authority, and by derogation another relevant authority may be identified in appropriate circumstances with coordination ensured [3]. The excerpts do not list the specific national authority in any Member State, and they do not cover the full scope of authority powers or the Article 74 rules for AI systems used by Union institutions, which are assigned to the European Data Protection Supervisor [5]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Providers must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system [2, Art. 72(1)]. The system must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data, which may be provided by deployers or collected from other sources, on the performance of the system throughout its lifetime, to evaluate continuous compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements [2, Art. 72(2)]. Where relevant, it must include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems [2, Art. 72(2); 1, Recital 154]. It must be based on a post-market monitoring plan that forms part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV [2, Art. 72(3)]. The Commission is to adopt an implementing act setting a template and list of plan elements by 2 February 2026 [2, Art. 72(3)]. The obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law-enforcement authorities [2, Art. 72(2); 1, Recital 154]. Providers should also have a system to report serious incidents to the relevant authorities [1, Recital 155]. The excerpts do not cover the provisions for high-risk AI systems already subject to Annex I Section A legislation beyond the start of Art. 72(4), nor the full serious-incident reporting obligations under Article 73.

Under Article 73 the report must be provided immediately, and not later than two days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the incident [1]. Where a person has died, paragraph 4 applies 'notwithstanding' the general rule: the report must be provided immediately after the provider or deployer has established, or as soon as it suspects, a causal relationship between the high-risk AI system and the serious incident, but not later than 10 days after becoming aware of the serious incident [1]. Where necessary to ensure timely reporting, an incomplete initial report may be submitted, followed by a complete report [1]. The excerpt does not show the full opening text of Article 73, so the exact paragraph numbering of the two-day rule is not confirmed, and the excerpts do not cover how 'serious incident' is defined beyond a reference to Article 3(49)(c).
unsupported_claims: The two-day rule is located in paragraph 2 of Article 73.
contradicted_points: The system answer states the general deadline is two days after awareness, contradicting the 15-day general deadline in the reference

items.answer: The excerpts do not contain the operative provision on a right to explanation of individual decisions (in the Act this is generally Article 86, which is not among the excerpts). They only mention in recitals that the difficulty in obtaining meaningful information on how such systems function and challenging their results in court can impact defence rights of suspects [4], and that lack of transparency, explainability and documentation could hamper the right to an effective remedy and fair trial [6]. They do not establish a specific right to an explanation, its scope, or its conditions, so the question cannot be fully answered from these excerpts. This is information about the law, not legal advice.
contexts: Annex III, point 8 – Annex IV, point 1
unsupported_claims: The excerpts establish a specific right to an explanation, its scope, or its conditions.
The answer is information about the law and not legal advice.
contradicted_points: Yes, a right to an explanation exists for persons affected by decisions based on AI system output

items.answer: Under Article 85 (the excerpts show the text under the heading Article 84(1)–Article 86(2)), any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the provisions of the Regulation may submit complaints to the relevant market surveillance authority, without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies [1]. Such complaints are taken into account for market surveillance activities under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and handled under the market surveillance authorities' dedicated procedures [1]. Downstream providers have a specific right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement concerning general-purpose AI models with the AI Office, which must be duly reasoned and indicate at least the point of contact of the provider, a description of the relevant facts, and the relevant provisions [2]. The excerpts do not specify the contact details or procedure for filing, which would need to be checked with the relevant national market surveillance authority or the AI Office.
unsupported_claims: The complaint for downstream providers is lodged with the AI Office.

items.answer: The excerpts do not state the maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice. They include Article 3 and the start of Article 5(1) (prohibiting, for example, AI systems deploying subliminal or manipulative techniques) and Recital 168, which says fines should take into account the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and the size of the provider, including SMEs. They do not contain the Article 99 penalty amounts for prohibited practices, so the maximum amount cannot be stated from these excerpts.

Under Article 99(5), supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For SMEs, including start-ups, the fine is up to whichever of those percentages or amounts is lower (Article 99(6)) [1]. Separately, for providers of general-purpose AI models, Article 101(1) provides fines of up to 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where the provider supplies incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request under Article 91 [2]. The excerpts do not cover the Commission's fine regime in full detail beyond this, and they do not state how the fine is calculated for every case beyond the factors listed in Article 99(7) [1][5].

The excerpts do not state the fine amounts. They refer to fines 'in accordance with Article 99' (excerpts 1 and 5 context, Article 80(4) and 80(7)) and to Member States setting fines taking into account the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and the size of the provider, including SMEs and start-ups [6]. Article 99 itself, which contains the maximum amounts, is not included in the excerpts, so the specific fine ceilings for non-compliance with high-risk obligations cannot be stated from them.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts state the specific maximum fine amounts for non-compliance with high-risk AI system obligations.

items.answer: The excerpts show that the Commission may impose fines and periodic penalty payments under Article 101(1) on providers of general-purpose AI models, including where a provider fails to give the Commission access to the model for an evaluation under Article 92 [1]. The amount is fixed having regard to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, applying the principles of proportionality and appropriateness, and the Commission must also take account of commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56 [1]. Before adopting such a decision, the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings and give the provider an opportunity to be heard [1]. Fines must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive [1]. Fines may also be imposed under Article 101 for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request for information [6]. The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review fining decisions and may cancel, reduce or increase the fine [1]. The excerpts do not state the maximum fine amounts or percentages, so the specific ceilings are not covered and would need to be checked in the full text of Article 101.

Yes. Article 100 (in excerpts [3] and [2]) provides that the European Data Protection Supervisor may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of the Regulation [3]. Recital (168) also states that the EDPS should have the power to impose such fines on Union institutions, agencies and bodies within the Regulation's scope [1]. Article 100(2) sets fines of up to EUR 1 500 000 for non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibitions, and Article 100(3) sets fines of up to EUR 750 000 for non-compliance of an AI system with other requirements or obligations [2]. Before deciding, the EDPS must give the institution concerned the opportunity to be heard [2]. When setting the amount, the EDPS must consider factors such as nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, and the degree of responsibility of the institution [3][2]. Decisions are subject to review by the Court of Justice of the EU [1]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed procedure beyond these points.

The excerpts give a partial timeline. The Regulation should apply from 2 August 2026 [1], but the prohibitions and the general provisions should already apply from 2 February 2025 [1]. The provisions on notified bodies and governance structure, and the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, apply from 2 August 2025 [1]. The provisions on penalties apply from 2 August 2025 [5]. Codes of practice should be ready by 2 May 2025 [1]. Each Member State must have at least one AI regulatory sandbox operational by 2 August 2026 [4]. Transitional rules: providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027 [2]; high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 are covered only if they undergo significant changes in design, and systems used by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 [2]; AI systems that are components of large-scale IT systems in Annex X placed on the market before 2 August 2027 must comply by 31 December 2030 [3]. The excerpts do not cover the application dates of every Article, such as the high-risk obligations in Chapter III or the Annex I product-linked rules in full, so those are not fully addressed here.

Yes, but with a later deadline. Article 111(3) states that providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply with the obligations in the Regulation by 2 August 2027 [4]. Recital (177) notes that obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models apply from 2 August 2025 for new models [1]. The excerpts do not state the full list of obligations that apply to these pre-existing models, nor whether any other exceptions apply beyond the general exception for open-source models noted in Recital (104)-(105), which does not exclude systemic-risk models [3].
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not state the full list of obligations that apply to pre-existing general-purpose AI models.

items.answer: Yes. Article 95(1) provides that Member States shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct intended to foster the voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, taking into account available technical solutions and industry best practices [2]. Article 95(2) adds that the AI Office and the Member States shall facilitate codes of conduct on the voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems, based on clear objectives and key performance indicators, covering elements such as Union ethical guidelines for trustworthy AI, environmental sustainability, AI literacy, inclusive and diverse design, and assessing and preventing negative impacts on vulnerable persons, including accessibility and gender equality [2]. Article 95(3) states that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or other relevant entities [2]. Recital (165) encourages providers and, as appropriate, deployers of all AI systems, high-risk or not, and AI models to apply such additional requirements voluntarily, and says that voluntary codes of conduct should be based on clear objectives and key performance indicators and developed inclusively [1]. The excerpts do not set out the full detail of the codes' governance mechanisms or the rules on their adoption and evaluation, so those points are not covered here.

Yes, in part. Recital (171) states that persons acting as whistleblowers on infringements of the Regulation should be protected under Union law, and that Directive (EU) 2019/1937 should therefore apply to the reporting of infringements of the Regulation and to the protection of persons reporting such infringements [1]. Article 87 repeats that Directive (EU) 2019/1937 shall apply to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements [2]. The excerpts do not contain the operative content of Directive (EU) 2019/1937 (its protection measures or conditions), so the specific scope of that protection cannot be stated from them. Note that the excerpt labelled Article 87 is not clearly tied to a whistleblower provision in the text shown, so the reference rests on the recital and the sentence quoted in excerpt [2].
contexts: Annex I, point 20 – Annex III, point 1
unsupported_claims: Article 87 repeats that Directive (EU) 2019/1937 shall apply to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements.

items.answer: The excerpts describe the AI Office mainly as the Commission's body for monitoring general-purpose AI models. It can take the necessary actions to monitor the effective implementation of and compliance with the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models [2][5]. It can investigate possible infringements on its own initiative, following its monitoring results, or upon request from market surveillance authorities [5]. Its investigative powers include requesting documentation and information and conducting evaluations, and it may involve independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf [2]. Enforcement measures include requests to take appropriate measures, including risk mitigation for identified systemic risks, and restricting the making available on the market, withdrawing or recalling the model [2]. Providers of general-purpose AI models have procedural rights under Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, applied mutatis mutandis, as a safeguard [2]. Downstream providers may lodge complaints about possible infringements, and a scientific panel of independent experts supports the AI Office's monitoring and may issue qualified alerts that trigger follow-ups such as investigations [5]. The excerpts do not set out the AI Office's full role for AI systems other than general-purpose AI models, nor the detailed text of its enforcement articles, so those aspects are not covered.

Yes, in part. For general-purpose AI models, compliance with European harmonised standards grants providers the presumption of conformity to the extent that those standards cover the relevant obligations (Article 53(4) [1]; Article 55(2) for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk [3]). Providers who do not comply with a European harmonised standard must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission [1][3]. Recital (121) states that harmonised standards, normally expected to reflect the state of the art, should be a means for providers to demonstrate conformity with the Regulation's requirements [6]. Recital (123) also states that high-risk AI systems certified under a cybersecurity scheme whose references are published in the Official Journal should be presumed to comply with the cybersecurity requirement, in so far as the certificate covers that requirement [4]. The excerpts do not set out the full presumption rules for high-risk AI systems generally, so the scope beyond these provisions is not covered.

Under Article 79(2), where a market surveillance authority, after evaluating the AI system for compliance with all requirements and obligations of the Regulation, finds that it does not comply, it must without undue delay require the relevant operator to take all appropriate corrective actions to bring the AI system into compliance, to withdraw the AI system from the market, or to recall it, within a period the authority may prescribe and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period provided for in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation [1]. The market surveillance authority must inform the relevant notified body accordingly [1]. Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies to these measures [1]. Where risks to fundamental rights are identified, the authority must also inform and fully cooperate with the relevant national public authorities or bodies referred to in Article 77(1), and particular attention must be given to AI systems presenting a risk to vulnerable groups [1]. Relevant operators must cooperate as necessary with the authority [1]. For AI systems classified by the provider as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) that the authority finds to be high-risk, Article 80 requires the provider to bring the system into compliance and take corrective action within a period the authority may prescribe, and the authority must inform the Commission and other Member States if use is not restricted to its national territory [2]. The excerpts do not cover the full procedure for cases where the provider fails to act, beyond the start of that provision [2].

Yes, in general. Market surveillance authorities must treat any information or documentation they obtain in accordance with the confidentiality obligations in Article 78 [1]. Under Article 78, the authorities involved must request only data strictly necessary for assessing the risk posed by AI systems and for exercising their powers, must put in place adequate and effective cybersecurity measures to protect the security and confidentiality of the information obtained, and must delete the data once it is no longer needed for the purpose for which it was obtained [3]. Information exchanged confidentially between national competent authorities, or between them and the Commission, may not be disclosed without prior consultation of the originating national competent authority and, where relevant, the deployer, where high-risk systems of Annex III points 1, 6 or 7 are used by law enforcement, border control, immigration or asylum authorities and disclosure would jeopardise public and national security interests [3]. Technical documentation for such systems must remain within the premises of those authorities, and only staff holding the appropriate level of security clearance may access it [4]. Article 78 also states that its paragraphs do not affect the rights or obligations of the Commission, Member States, and notified bodies regarding information exchange and warnings, or obligations to provide information under criminal law [4]. The excerpts do not contain the full list of exceptions in Article 78(1), so the scope of those exceptions beyond the points shown (including public and national security, criminal or administrative proceedings and classified information) cannot be fully confirmed from these excerpts [3].

The excerpts do not contain the GDPR's maximum fine for a personal data breach. They cover AI Act administrative fines (e.g., Article 99 percentages and amounts, Article 100 EDPS fines for Union institutions, and Recitals 168-170), and only mention Regulation (EU) 2016/679 in passing (Article 10(5)(f) and Recital 69 referencing records of processing and Article 9(2)(g)). The GDPR penalty provisions are not included, so the question cannot be answered from these excerpts.

The excerpts do not contain any information about fees, charges or costs that a notified body may levy for certifying an AI system. They describe notified body independence (Article 31(4)), the Annex VII conformity assessment procedure (application, technical documentation examination, certificate issuance) and registration information (Annex VIII), but say nothing about pricing. Fee levels would need to be checked in the national rules of the relevant Member State or with the notified body itself.
contexts: Annex VIII, point 7 – Annex VIII, point 5

items.answer: The excerpts cover only the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and say nothing about US federal agencies or the regulation of AI in the United States, so the question cannot be answered from them.

The excerpts do not contain any information about European Parliament vote counts or the adoption procedure for the AI Act. They cover amendments to other Union legislation, Annex III and IV documentation requirements, Commission review obligations under Article 112 and recitals 174-176, and delegated-power provisions in Articles 96-97. Vote tallies would need to be sourced from the legislative record outside the provided excerpts.
contexts: Annex III, point 8 – Annex IV, point 1

items.answer: Article 5(1)(a) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness, or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting a person's or group's behaviour by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not otherwise have taken, in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm to that person, another person or a group [1]. Article 5(1)(b) separately prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm [1]. The excerpts do not include the full text of any further exceptions or the Commission guidance on interpreting 'significant harm'.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not include the full text of any further exceptions to the prohibitions.
The excerpts do not include Commission guidance on interpreting 'significant harm'.

items.answer: Generally no. Article 5(1)(c) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems that evaluate or classify natural persons over a period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the social score leads to either or both of: (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to where the data was originally generated or collected, or (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity [1]. The prohibition is framed generally and does not name governments, so it covers public authorities using such systems. The excerpts do not include the rest of Article 5, any exceptions, or enforcement and penalty provisions, so I cannot confirm whether any other carve-outs apply. This is information about the law, not legal advice.
contexts: Annex III, point 3 – Annex III, point 4
unsupported_claims: The Article 5(1)(c) prohibition is framed generally and does not name governments, so it covers public authorities using such systems.

items.answer: Generally no. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or using AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions [4]. The only exception stated in the excerpt is where the use is intended for medical or safety reasons [4]. Note that Article 50(3) separately requires deployers of emotion recognition systems to inform the natural persons exposed to them, but that transparency duty does not make such use permitted where Article 5(1)(f) applies [3][4]. The excerpts do not show how 'medical or safety reasons' is interpreted, nor the penalties or enforcement details, so those points are not covered here. This is general information about the law, not legal advice.
contexts: Annex III, point 3 – Annex III, point 4

items.answer: No. Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage [1]. The excerpts do not contain any exception to this prohibition, so they do not indicate that such a database could be built this way lawfully. Targeted (not untargeted) collection, and any other activities outside this specific prohibited purpose, are not addressed by the excerpts. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Partly. Article 5(1)(h) prohibits the use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, unless and in so far as such use is strictly necessary for one of the objectives listed in that point [1]. Under Article 5(2), such use is deployed only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual, and the authority must consider the nature of the situation (seriousness, probability and scale of harm if the system were not used) and the consequences for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned [2][3]. Use must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards under national law, in particular as regards temporal, geographic and personal limitations [2]. It may be authorised only if the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49; in duly justified cases of urgency it may start before registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay [2]. Article 26(10) adds that such post-remote biometric identification systems may not be used in an untargeted way without a link to a criminal offence, a criminal proceeding, a genuine and present or foreseeable threat of a criminal offence, or the search for a specific missing person, and no adverse legal decision may be based solely on their output; each use must be documented in the police file [4]. The excerpts do not list the enumerated objectives in Article 5(1)(h), so the specific permitted purposes are not covered here. This is general information, not legal advice.

Yes, in general. Article 5(1)(g) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individual natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation [1]. A biometric categorisation system is defined as an AI system for assigning natural persons to specific categories on the basis of their biometric data, unless it is ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons [4]. The prohibition does not cover labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data, or categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement [1]. Article 5(1)(g) is the relevant provision; the excerpts do not include the full text of any further exceptions beyond those stated there. This is information about the law, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not include the full text of any further exceptions beyond those stated in Article 5(1)(g).

items.answer: No, not in the circumstances described. Article 5(1)(d) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or using an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, where this is based solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics [1]. The prohibition does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of a person's involvement in a criminal activity, where that assessment is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity [1]. The excerpts do not cover other AI uses for crime prediction beyond this provision, nor any broader rules on profiling outside Article 5(1)(d).

Partly yes. Article 5(1)(b) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation [1]. The prohibition applies where the objective or effect is materially distorting the behaviour of that person or a group member in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm [1]. Children are covered by the age criterion and disabled persons by the disability criterion, so the ban is not general: it requires both the exploitation of vulnerability and the materially distorting, significant-harm effect. The excerpts do not contain any further exceptions to Article 5(1)(b), nor any guidance on how 'significant harm' or 'materially distorting' is assessed, so those points are not covered.

The excerpts do not list the serious crimes. They refer to the objectives in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h), but the text of that point (which would name the objectives, such as searching for victims or preventing threats) is not included. Article 5(2) and 5(3) describe conditions such as strict necessity, proportionality, and prior authorisation [1][5], and Article 5(2) requires use only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual [1], but none of the excerpts specify which offences qualify. Article 5(1)(h) and its referenced crime list would need to be retrieved to answer this.
unsupported_claims: The text of Article 5(1)(h) names objectives such as searching for victims or preventing threats.

items.answer: Article 3(1) defines an 'AI system' as 'a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments' [1]. The excerpts do not include any further guidance or exclusions on this definition.

The excerpts do not contain the definition of 'deployer'. They show obligations that apply to deployers of high-risk AI systems (Article 26 and Article 27), but the defining provision (Article 3 definitions) is not among the excerpts, so the definition cannot be stated from them.

The excerpts do not contain the definition of 'general-purpose AI model'. They only cover Article 53(1)(d) (training content summary), Article 75 (AI Office powers), Article 51 (classification as general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, including the 10^25 FLOP presumption), Article 101 (fines), Annex XII point 1 (transparency information) and Article 53(5)-(7). The definition itself, which is normally found in Article 3 of the Regulation, was not retrieved and is needed to answer the question.
unsupported_claims: The definition of general-purpose AI model is normally found in Article 3 of the Regulation.

items.answer: Under Article 3, point (60), a 'deep fake' means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful [1]. Article 50(4) requires deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates deep fake content to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, subject to the exceptions stated there, including use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, and a limited disclosure approach for evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works [2].

Not in general. Under Article 2(3) the Regulation does not apply to AI systems where and in so far as they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities [1]. The same paragraph also excludes AI systems not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for those purposes [1]. The exclusion is limited to systems used exclusively for these purposes; the excerpts do not cover AI systems with mixed civil and military use, and the excerpts do not state how the exclusion applies to dual-use systems.

The excerpts do not contain the AI Act's scope provision (normally Article 2, which addresses who and what the Regulation applies to, including exclusions for purely personal non-professional activity). The retrieved excerpts only cover prohibited practices (Article 5(1)), technical documentation (Annex IV, point 2), value chain responsibilities (Article 25(4)), transparency (Article 50(1)) and fundamental rights impact assessments (Article 27(5)), so I cannot confirm whether personal hobby use is excluded. Please retrieve the scope provisions, and note that this is information about the law, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The AI Act's scope provision (normally Article 2) addresses who and what the Regulation applies to, including exclusions for purely personal non-professional activity.

items.answer: No, not for AI systems or AI models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development; the Regulation does not apply to them, including their output [1] (Article 2(6)). Related exclusion: the Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to being placed on the market or put into service, but testing in real world conditions is not covered by that exclusion [1] (Article 2(8)). The excerpts do not state whether an AI system built for research that is later placed on the market or put into service remains outside scope, so that point cannot be confirmed from them.

Yes, in principle. Article 2(1)(c) applies the Regulation to providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country (such as the US), where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union [3]. Article 2(1)(a) also covers providers placing AI systems on the market or putting them into service in the Union irrespective of whether they are established in the Union or in a third country [3]. Exclusions may still apply: the Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as systems falling under Article 5 or 50 [1]; it does not apply to AI systems used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes [4]; and it does not apply to research, testing or development activity before placing on the market or putting into service, although testing in real world conditions is not covered by that exclusion [6]. The excerpts do not cover the specific obligations that would apply to a given company, so a full assessment of its role (provider, deployer, etc.) and of other applicable exemptions would require the complete text. This is general information, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not cover the specific obligations that would apply to a given company.

items.answer: Article 4 requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf [1]. The measures must take into account those persons' technical knowledge, experience, education and training, the context in which the AI systems are to be used, and the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used [1]. The regulation defines AI literacy as skills, knowledge and understanding that allow providers, deployers and affected persons, taking into account their respective rights and obligations, to make an informed deployment of AI systems and to gain awareness about the opportunities and risks of AI and possible harm it can cause [2]. The excerpts do not specify what concrete measures or training content are required, nor any enforcement details or dates.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not specify what concrete measures or training content are required.
The excerpts do not specify enforcement details or dates for the AI literacy obligation.

items.answer: Under Article 6(1), an AI system is considered high-risk, irrespective of whether it is placed on the market or put into service independently of the products referred to, where both conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I [2]; and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation [2]. Under Article 6(2), in addition to those systems, AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk [2]. Article 6(3) provides a derogation: an Annex III system is not considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and this applies where one of conditions (a) to (d) is fulfilled, such as a narrow procedural task or a preparatory task to an assessment [1]. However, an Annex III system always remains high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons [1]. The excerpts do not include the text of Annex I or Annex III, so the specific use cases and product legislation are not covered.

Yes, but only under a narrow derogation. Under Article 6(3), an AI system referred to in Annex III is not considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making [1]. The derogation applies where at least one condition is met: the system performs a narrow procedural task, is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the completed human assessment absent proper human review, or is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to Annex III use cases [1]. However, an Annex III system shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons [1]. A provider who considers an Annex III system not high-risk must document its assessment before placing it on the market or putting it into service, is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must provide the documentation to national competent authorities on request [3]. Separately, the Commission may by delegated act amend Annex III to remove high-risk systems only where they no longer pose any significant risks and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection [5]. The excerpts do not include the Commission's guidelines or examples referred to in Article 6(5), so practical application is not covered [3].

Yes, as a general rule. Annex III, point 4(a) lists AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates [1]. Under Article 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk [6]. However, Article 6(3) provides a derogation: an Annex III system shall not be considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making [2]. This applies where one of the conditions (a) to (d) is fulfilled, such as performing a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment without proper human review, or performing a preparatory task to an assessment [2]. The derogation does not apply where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk [2]. A provider who classifies such a system as non-high-risk may be required to justify this, and a market surveillance authority may evaluate the classification and require compliance if it finds the system is high-risk [3]. The excerpts do not include the full text of Article 6(3) conditions beyond those listed, nor the specific obligations that apply to high-risk systems, so these are not covered here.
citations: Annex III, point 3 – Annex III, point 4
contexts: Annex III, point 3 – Annex III, point 4
unsupported_claims: A provider who classifies such a system as non-high-risk may be required to justify this.

items.answer: Yes, generally. Annex III, point 5(b) lists AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score as high-risk, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud [1]. Under Article 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk [3]. However, Article 6(3) provides a derogation: an Annex III system is not considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and one of the listed conditions (a) to (d) applies [2]. Article 6(3) also states that an Annex III system shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons [2]. Credit scoring systems that profile natural persons therefore remain high-risk even if the derogation conditions would otherwise apply [2]. The excerpts do not cover the full requirements that apply to high-risk systems beyond the examples provided, nor the timing of application of these obligations.

Likely yes, under Annex III, point 3(d): AI systems intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels are listed as high-risk [1]. Software that monitors students for cheating during exams falls within that wording, since cheating is a form of prohibited behaviour during tests. Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decision making, and the derogation applies where a listed condition is met (narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing human assessment, or a preparatory task) [3]. However, the excerpt states that an Annex III system shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons [3]. The excerpts do not state how 'prohibited behaviour' or 'profiling' is defined, so whether a specific product is covered depends on its intended purpose and facts, and this is not legal advice.
citations: Annex III, point 3 – Annex III, point 4
contexts: Annex III, point 3 – Annex III, point 4
unsupported_claims: Software that monitors students for cheating during exams falls within the wording of Annex III, point 3(d) because cheating is a form of prohibited behaviour during tests.

items.answer: Under Annex III, point 5(c), AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance are high-risk [2], and under Article 6(2) AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk [3]. Only life and health insurance is covered by the excerpts; other insurance types (e.g., property or motor insurance) are not addressed in the excerpts. Article 6(3) provides a derogation: an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and the conditions (a) to (d) apply; however, an Annex III system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons [4]. Article 80 covers market surveillance authority evaluation of systems a provider classified as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) [1].

Annex III, point 7 lists high-risk AI systems in migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law [1]. These are: (a) AI systems used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or EU institutions, bodies, offices or agencies as polygraphs or similar tools [1]; (b) AI systems used by or on behalf of such authorities to assess a risk, including a security, irregular migration or health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or has entered a Member State's territory [1]; (c) AI systems used to assist such authorities in examining applications for asylum, visa or residence permits and associated complaints regarding the eligibility of applicants, including related assessments of the reliability of evidence [1]; and (d) AI systems used by or on behalf of such authorities, or by Union bodies, in migration, asylum or border control management to detect, recognise or identify natural persons, with the exception of verification of travel documents [1]. The excerpts do not include the full text of Article 6 or the wider classification rules, so they do not address any exceptions beyond these points. Related registration and oversight rules for these systems, such as the secure non-public EU database registration under Article 49(4) and the exemption from separate two-person verification under Article 14(5), are also noted in [2][6].
contexts: Annex VIII, point 10 – Annex VIII, point 6

items.answer: Yes, but only by delegated act. Under Article 7(1), the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems [1]. Two conditions must both be fulfilled: (a) the AI systems are intended to be used in any of the areas listed in Annex III; and (b) they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III [1]. The excerpts do not cover the criteria or procedure beyond these conditions, or the detailed content of Article 97.

Partly. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk if it is intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, or is itself such a product, and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service [1]. Machinery is covered: Directive 2006/42/EC on machinery is listed in Annex I, Section A, point 1 [4]. So an AI safety component in machinery is high-risk if the machinery also requires third-party conformity assessment under that directive, which the excerpts do not state. For medical devices, the excerpts do not include the Annex I entries for Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746. Article 73(10) refers to high-risk AI systems that are safety components of devices covered by those regulations [2], but that provision concerns serious-incident reporting and does not itself state the high-risk classification. Article 25(3) also treats the product manufacturer as provider in certain Annex I cases [3]. Confirming the medical device position needs the full Annex I text and Article 6(1)'s conformity assessment condition.
citations: Annex I, point 1 – Annex I, point 6
contexts: Annex I, point 1 – Annex I, point 6
Annex III, point 1 – Annex III, point 2
unsupported_claims: Article 73(10) itself states that medical-device AI safety components are high-risk.

items.answer: Under Article 9, the risk management system must be established, implemented, documented and maintained for high-risk AI systems [1]. It is a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle, requiring regular systematic review and updating [1]. It must comprise these steps: (a) identification and analysis of the known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights when used in accordance with the intended purpose; (b) estimation and evaluation of risks that may emerge under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; (c) evaluation of other possibly arising risks, based on data from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72; and (d) adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures addressing the risks identified under point (a) [1]. The risks covered are only those that may be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through development or design, or through adequate technical information [1]. High-risk AI systems must also be tested to identify the most appropriate measures, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds, before being placed on the market or put into service [2]. Providers must consider whether the system is likely to adversely impact persons under 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups [2]. Providers subject to other Union law risk management requirements may combine these aspects with those procedures [2]. Not covered by these excerpts: the full list of testing and documentation details beyond Article 9(1)-(3), (6)-(10), and the Article 9(4)-(5) provisions.

Under Article 10(3), training, validation and testing data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose [2]. They must have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used; these characteristics may be met at the level of individual data sets or a combination thereof [2]. Under Article 10(4), data sets must take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting in which the system is intended to be used [2]. These criteria apply under Article 10(1) to high-risk AI systems that use techniques involving training of AI models with data, whenever such data sets are used [1]. Article 10(2) also requires data governance and management practices covering matters such as design choices, data collection and origin, preparation, assumptions, and examination and mitigation of possible biases [5]. The excerpts do not provide the full text of Article 10(5), so any criteria in that paragraph are not covered.

Yes, but only exceptionally. Under Article 10(5), providers of high-risk AI systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data (which would include ethnicity, as a special category, though the excerpts do not list the categories expressly) to the extent strictly necessary for ensuring bias detection and correction under Article 10(2)(f) and (g), subject to appropriate safeguards for fundamental rights and freedoms [1]. All listed conditions must be met: bias detection cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data; technical limitations on re-use, state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures including pseudonymisation apply; access is strictly controlled and documented; the data must not be transmitted, transferred or accessed by other parties [1]; the data must be deleted once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first; and records of processing must explain why processing was strictly necessary and why other data could not achieve the objective [2]. The Regulation (EU) 2016/679, 2018/1725 and Directive 2016/680 rules also continue to apply in addition [1]. The excerpts do not confirm that ethnicity specifically is a special category, and they do not cover the wider GDPR legal basis analysis.
unsupported_claims: Ethnicity is a special category of personal data.
The excerpts do not cover the wider GDPR legal basis analysis.

items.answer: Under Article 11(1), the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system must be drawn up before the system is placed on the market or put into service, kept up-to date, and drawn up to demonstrate compliance with the requirements in Section 2 and to give national competent authorities and notified bodies the necessary information in a clear and comprehensive form to assess compliance [1]. At a minimum it must contain the elements set out in Annex IV [1]. SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the Annex IV elements in a simplified manner using the simplified form the Commission is to establish, and notified bodies must accept that form for conformity assessment [1]. Where a high-risk AI system is related to a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, a single set of technical documentation must contain all Article 11(1) information plus the information required under those legal acts [2]. The Commission may amend Annex IV by delegated act under Article 97 to reflect technical progress [2]. The excerpts do not set out the full content of Annex IV itself, so the specific Annex IV elements are not listed here.

Yes. Article 12(1) requires that high-risk AI systems technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system [1]. The logging capabilities must enable recording of events relevant for identifying situations that may result in a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or a substantial modification, facilitating post-market monitoring under Article 72, and monitoring operation under Article 26(5) [1]. For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, logs must at minimum record the period of each use, the reference database checked, the input data matching the search, and the identity of natural persons involved in verifying results under Article 14(5) [1]. Providers must keep the automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise, in particular under data protection law [2]. Deployers have a parallel obligation to keep logs under their control for at least six months, subject to the same exceptions [3]. Providers must give competent authorities access to these logs upon a reasoned request, to the extent they are under their control [4]. The excerpts do not cover how the logging requirement applies beyond these provisions or any penalties for non-compliance.

Under Article 13(3), the instructions for use must contain at least the following information [1][2]: (a) the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative [1]; (b) the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the system, including its intended purpose, the level of accuracy (including metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15) and any known and foreseeable circumstances affecting it, any known or foreseeable circumstances related to use (including reasonably foreseeable misuse) that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2), where applicable the technical capabilities to explain output, when appropriate performance regarding specific persons or groups, when appropriate input data specifications or relevant information on training, validation and testing data sets, and where applicable information enabling deployers to interpret and appropriately use the output [1][2]; (c) pre-determined changes to the system and its performance, if any, set at the initial conformity assessment [2]; (d) the human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs [2]; (e) the computational and hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and necessary maintenance and care measures including their frequency, including software updates [2]; and (f) where relevant, a description of log collection, storage and interpretation mechanisms under Article 12 [2]. Under Article 13(2), the instructions must be concise, complete, correct and clear, relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers [3]. The excerpts do not cover any further detail on how these items must be presented beyond this.

Under Article 14(1)-(3), high-risk AI systems must be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use [2]. Oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, including under reasonably foreseeable misuse [2]. Measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and are ensured through measures built into the system by the provider where technically feasible and/or measures identified by the provider that are appropriate for the deployer to implement [2]. Under Article 14(4), the system must be provided to the deployer so that overseers can properly understand its capacities and limitations and monitor its operation, stay aware of automation bias, correctly interpret output, decide not to use or to override or reverse the output, and intervene or interrupt the system via a 'stop' button or similar procedure bringing it to a safe state, as appropriate and proportionate [1]. Article 26(2) requires deployers to assign oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support [5]. Article 14(5) adds, for Annex III point 1(a) biometric identification systems, that no action or decision may be taken on the basis of the identification unless separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons, with an exception for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum where Union or national law deems this disproportionate [6]. The excerpts do not cover further technical details of how these measures must be implemented.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not cover further technical details of how these measures must be implemented.

items.answer: Article 15(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle [1]. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics must be declared in the accompanying instructions of use [1], and Article 13(3)(b)(ii) requires the instructions for use to state the accuracy level, metrics, robustness and cybersecurity against which the system was tested and validated [3]. Article 15(2) provides that the Commission shall encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies [1]. Robustness: under Article 15(4), high-risk AI systems must be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies, with technical and organisational measures, and redundancy solutions such as backup or fail-safe plans may be used [2]; systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market must address feedback loops with appropriate mitigation [2]. Cybersecurity: under Article 15(5), high-risk AI systems must be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities, with solutions appropriate to the circumstances and risks, including, where appropriate, measures against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks or model flaws [4]. Annex IV, point 2(g) and (h) require technical documentation to include the metrics used to measure accuracy and robustness, the test reports, and the cybersecurity measures put in place [6]. Article 8(1) requires compliance with these requirements in light of the intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art [5]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed content of the risk management system under Article 9 or conformity assessment procedures.

The excerpts only partly answer this. Article 16 sets out some provider obligations: upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, providers must demonstrate conformity of the high-risk AI system with the Section 2 requirements [4], and must ensure the system complies with accessibility requirements under Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882 [4]. Article 25(4) requires the provider and any third-party supplier of tools, services, components or processes used or integrated in a high-risk AI system to specify, by written agreement, the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance so the provider can fully comply with the Regulation; this does not apply to third parties making accessible to the public tools, services, processes or components, other than general-purpose AI models, under a free and open-source licence [5]. Article 25(1) explains when distributors, importers, deployers or other third parties become providers subject to Article 16 obligations, e.g. by putting their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system, making a substantial modification, or modifying the intended purpose so the system becomes high-risk [3]. Article 25(2) states that an initial provider that is no longer considered a provider in those circumstances must closely cooperate with new providers and supply necessary information and reasonably expected technical access [1]. The excerpts do not contain the full list of Article 16 obligations (lettters a to j, including quality management, documentation, logging, risk management, conformity assessment and registration), so those are not covered here.

Under Article 17(1), a provider of high-risk AI systems must put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation, documented systematically in written policies, procedures and instructions [2][5][6]. At least the following aspects must be included: a strategy for regulatory compliance, including conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications [5]; techniques and procedures for design, design control and design verification, and for development, quality control and quality assurance [5]; examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, with their frequency [5]; technical specifications and standards applied, and the means used where harmonised standards are not fully applied [5]; data management systems and procedures [6]; the risk management system under Article 9 [6]; a post-market monitoring system under Article 72 [6]; procedures for reporting serious incidents under Article 73 [6]; handling of communication with authorities, notified bodies, operators, customers and other interested parties [6]; record-keeping systems [6]; resource management, including security-of-supply measures [6]; and an accountability framework setting out management and staff responsibilities [2]. The implementation must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, while respecting the required degree of rigour and level of protection [4]. Providers subject to sectoral Union law may include these aspects within existing quality management systems under that law [4]. For financial institutions, the obligation is deemed fulfilled by complying with internal governance rules under Union financial services law, except for points (g), (h) and (i) of Article 17(1) [4]. For conformity assessment via Annex VII, the notified body assesses whether the quality management system meets Article 17 requirements [3][1]. The excerpts do not cover the full text of Article 17(1)(a) to (m) beyond what is quoted, nor the details of Article 9, 72 or 73.

Under Article 18(1), the provider must keep the listed documentation (technical documentation under Article 11, quality management system documentation under Article 17, documentation on changes approved by notified bodies where applicable, notified body decisions and documents where applicable, and the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47) for a period ending 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service, available to national competent authorities [1]. Article 18(2) requires each Member State to set conditions for keeping this documentation available for that period if a provider or its authorised representative established on its territory goes bankrupt or ceases activity earlier [1]. Under Article 18(3), providers that are financial institutions subject to Union financial services law requirements may maintain the technical documentation as part of the documentation kept under that law [1]. Separately, Article 19(1) requires providers to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, which is a different obligation from the 10-year documentation period [2].

The excerpts give a minimum period of at least six months for both providers and deployers. Providers must keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, to the extent they are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, of at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise, in particular Union data protection law [1]. Deployers have the same obligation: they must keep the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise [2]. Financial institutions subject to Union financial services law instead keep the logs as part of the documentation required under that financial services law [1][2]. The excerpts do not state an upper limit on the retention period, and the logs must be automatically recorded over the system's lifetime under Article 12(1) [3].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the systems in accordance with the instructions for use [1]. They must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support [1]. To the extent they control input data, they must ensure it is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose [1]. They must monitor operation based on the instructions for use and, where relevant, inform providers under Article 72; if they have reason to consider use may present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), they must without undue delay inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority and suspend use; for serious incidents they must immediately inform first the provider, then the importer or distributor and the market surveillance authorities [2]. Deployers that are public authorities or Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies must comply with the registration obligations in Article 49 and must not use a high-risk system not registered in the EU database under Article 71, informing the provider or distributor [3]. Where applicable, they must use information provided under Article 13 for data protection impact assessments under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 [3]. Deployers of Annex III systems that make or assist decisions about natural persons must inform those persons they are subject to the system, without prejudice to Article 50 [4]. They must cooperate with competent authorities [4]. Under Article 27, deployers must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, notify the market surveillance authority of its results, and update it when elements change [5]. The excerpts do not cover all deployer obligations, such as those in other provisions beyond Article 26 and 27, or the full content of Article 13 instructions for use beyond the transparency principle [6].

Yes, if you are a deployer who is an employer. Under Article 26(7), before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, deployers who are employers must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system [1]. This information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures in Union and national law and practice on informing workers and their representatives [1]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed content or format of that information beyond this, nor any consequences of non-compliance.

Under Article 27(1), deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2) [1][3]. The obligation does not apply to high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III [1][3]. Under Article 27(2), it applies to the first use of the system, and deployers may in similar cases rely on previously conducted assessments or existing assessments carried out by the provider [2].
