The excerpts do not cover the remaining deployers outside these categories, or the full detail of the Article 6(2) and Annex III references beyond what is quoted.

Under Article 22(1), before making its high-risk AI system available on the Union market, a provider established in a third country must, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union [1]. Under Article 22(2), the provider must enable that authorised representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate [1]. Article 3(5) defines an authorised representative as a natural or legal person established in the Union who has received and accepted a written mandate from the provider to perform and carry out its obligations and procedures under the Regulation on its behalf [5]. The excerpts do not cover the specific tasks that the mandate must contain, nor any further obligations of such providers beyond this appointment.

Under Article 23(1), before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, importers must ensure the system conforms to the Regulation by verifying that: (a) the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 has been carried out by the provider [1]; (b) the provider has drawn up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV [1]; (c) the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and instructions for use [1]; and (d) the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1) [1]. Under Article 23(2), if an importer has sufficient reason to consider the system is not in conformity, or is falsified or accompanied by falsified documentation, it must not place the system on the market until it has been brought into conformity [1]. The excerpts do not cover any further verification steps beyond these.

Yes, in that case. Under Article 25(1)(b), any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, in such a way that it remains a high-risk AI system under Article 6, is considered a provider of that high-risk AI system and is subject to the provider obligations under Article 16 [1]. Under Article 25(2), the initial provider then no longer counts as the provider of that specific system, but must closely cooperate with the new provider and provide the necessary information, reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, unless the initial provider clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk AI system [3]. Also, a high-risk AI system that has already undergone conformity assessment must undergo a new conformity assessment procedure in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether it is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer [2]. The excerpts do not define 'substantial modification' beyond the reference to Article 6, so whether a specific change qualifies is not covered. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Under Article 24, distributors of high-risk AI systems must: (1) before making a system available, verify it bears the required CE marking, is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and instructions for use, and that the provider and importer have complied with their obligations under Article 16(b) and (c) and Article 23(3) [2]; (2) not make the system available until it is brought into conformity if they consider or have reason to consider it non-conforming with Section 2, and inform the provider or importer if it presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) [2]; (3) ensure storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise conformity with Section 2 while the system is under their responsibility [2]; (4) where they consider or have reason to consider a system they have made available is non-conforming, take corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw or recall it, or ensure the provider, importer or relevant operator does so, and if it presents a risk under Article 79(1), immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities with details [3]; (5) upon a reasoned request from a competent authority, provide all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity [3]; and (6) cooperate with competent authorities in any action they take regarding the system, in particular to reduce or mitigate its risk [1]. Note that under Article 25(1), a distributor that puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose so the system becomes high-risk is treated as a provider with Article 16 obligations [4]. The excerpts do not cover the full text of Article 16, Article 23, or Article 79, so their specific contents are not set out here.

The excerpts only partly answer this. For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, the provider chooses between two procedures where it has applied harmonised standards (Article 40) or common specifications (Article 41): (a) internal control under Annex VI, or (b) assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation with a notified body under Annex VII [3]. Annex VII must be followed where harmonised standards do not exist and common specifications are not available, where the provider has not applied or has only partly applied the harmonised standard, where common specifications exist but were not applied, or where a restricted harmonised standard applies only to the restricted part [3]. For Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, except where law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies put the system into service, in which case the market surveillance authority under Article 74(8) or (9) acts as notified body [4]. For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, the procedure is internal control under Annex VI, without a notified body [2]. Annex VI requires the provider to verify its quality management system against Article 17, examine the technical documentation, and verify the design, development and post-market monitoring process [5]. The excerpts do not cover the conditions for Annex III point 1 systems beyond these points, nor the full text of Annex VII steps beyond points 4.4 and 4.5 [6]. Article 43 is the relevant provision.

contexts: Annex VI, point 1 – Annex VI, point 4

items.answer: Partly yes. Under Article 43(4), a high-risk AI system that has already undergone conformity assessment must undergo a new conformity assessment procedure in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer [1]. Changes that a provider pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment and that are part of the technical documentation referred to in point 2(f) of Annex IV do not constitute a substantial modification, for systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service [1]. For changes under Annex VII, any change that could affect compliance with the requirements or intended purpose must be assessed by the notified body that issued the Union technical documentation assessment certificate, which decides whether a new conformity assessment under Article 43(4) is required or whether the change can be handled by a supplement to the certificate [3]. The excerpts do not define the term 'substantial modification' or set out criteria for it, so whether a particular change qualifies cannot be determined from them.

Under Article 48(3), the CE marking shall be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly for high-risk AI systems [1]. Where that is not possible or not warranted due to the nature of the system, it shall instead be affixed to the packaging or to the accompanying documentation, as appropriate [1]. For high-risk AI systems provided digitally, a digital CE marking may be used only if it can easily be accessed via the interface from which the system is accessed or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means [1]. Where applicable, the CE marking shall be followed by the identification number of the notified body responsible for the conformity assessment under Article 43, and that number must also appear in promotional material stating the system fulfils CE marking requirements [1]. The CE marking is also subject to the general principles in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 [1]. Excerpts do not cover the full conformity assessment procedure or the detailed requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 that the marking indicates conformity with [3].
unsupported_claims: Excerpts do not cover the full conformity assessment procedure or the detailed requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 that the marking indicates conformity with.

items.answer: The provider must draw up a written, machine readable, physical or electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system, identifying that system, and it must state that the system meets the requirements of Section 2 [2]. It must contain the information set out in Annex V and be translated into a language easily understood by the national competent authorities of the Member States where the system is placed on the market or made available [2]. Under Annex V, it must contain: (1) the AI system name, type and any additional unambiguous reference for identification and traceability; (2) the name and address of the provider or authorised representative; (3) a statement that it is issued under the provider's sole responsibility; (4) a statement that the system conforms with the Regulation and any other applicable Union law requiring such a declaration; (5) where personal data is processed, a statement of compliance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680; (6) references to relevant harmonised standards or other common specifications used; (7) where applicable, the notified body's name and identification number, a description of the conformity assessment procedure, and identification of the certificate issued; and (8) the place and date of issue, the name and function of the signatory, an indication for whom they signed, and a signature [4]. Where several Union harmonisation laws require a declaration, a single declaration covering all of them may be drawn up [1]. By drawing it up, the provider assumes responsibility for compliance with Section 2, and must keep it up to date [1]. The provider must keep it at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service [2]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

contexts: Annex V, point 1 – Annex V, point 8

items.answer: Yes, in general. Under Article 49(1), before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 [2]. This applies with the exception of high-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III [2]. Article 71(1) states that the Commission, with the Member States, sets up and maintains this EU database for high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2) that are registered under Articles 49 and 60 [1]. Deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, or persons acting on their behalf, must also register themselves, select the system and register its use before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, again excluding point 2 of Annex III [2]. Article 26(8) adds that such public-sector deployers must not use a high-risk system they find is not registered and must inform the provider or distributor [3]. For high-risk systems in Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 in law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, registration is in a secure non-public section of the database and includes only limited information [5]. High-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III are registered at national level instead [5]. The excerpts do not set out the full content of the provider obligations beyond these provisions, so this answer is limited to the registration requirement. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

Yes, in general. Article 50(1) requires providers to ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system [1]. The obligation does not apply where this is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, taking into account the circumstances and context of use [1]. It also does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, unless those systems are available to the public to report a criminal offence [1]. The excerpts place this duty on providers rather than deployers, and do not address other transparency duties that may apply to a particular chatbot deployment beyond Article 50(1). This is information about the law, not legal advice.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts address transparency duties for a particular chatbot deployment beyond Article 50(1).

items.answer: Partly yes. Under Article 50(2), providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, as far as technically feasible [2]. This marking duty does not apply to the extent the systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences [2]. Separately, under Article 50(4), deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates a deep fake (image, audio or video) must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, subject to the criminal-law authorisation exception; for evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, disclosure is limited to its existence in a manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment of the work [1]. Deployers of AI generating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must also disclose this, unless authorised by law for criminal-law purposes or the content has undergone human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person holding editorial responsibility [1]. The excerpts do not give the detailed technical standards for watermarking or the dates when these obligations apply.

Deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system must inform the natural persons exposed to it of the operation of the system, and must process the personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable [1] (Article 50(3)). The disclosure obligation does not apply to AI systems used for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition that are permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties and in accordance with Union law [1] (Article 50(3)). The excerpts define these systems [2] (Article 3(39) and (40)) but do not cover any further details of what the notice must contain or how it must be given, so those points are not covered.
contexts: Annex III, point 1 – Annex III, point 2

items.answer: Under Article 51(2), a general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high impact capabilities (the Article 51(1)(a) condition) when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10^25 [1]. Article 51(1) states that a model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets either (a) high impact capabilities, evaluated using appropriate technical tools and methodologies, or (b) equivalent capabilities or impact, based on a Commission decision (ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel) having regard to Annex XIII [1]. The excerpts thus show that the 10^25 FLOP training-compute threshold triggers a presumption under Article 51(1)(a), while the 10^25 figure itself is only a presumption and the Commission may amend thresholds by delegated act under Article 51(3) [1]. Where a model meets the Article 51(1)(a) condition, the provider must notify the Commission within two weeks, and may submit substantiated arguments that, exceptionally, the model does not present systemic risks; the Commission may reject such arguments [5]. Annex XIII lists further designation criteria, including the presumption of high impact on the internal market where the model is made available to at least 10 000 registered business users established in the Union [3]. The excerpts do not state further detail on how the presumption may be rebutted beyond Article 52(2)-(3) as summarised here.
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not provide detail on how the presumption may be rebutted beyond Article 52(2)-(3) as summarised.

items.answer: Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk if it (a) has high impact capabilities, evaluated using appropriate technical tools and methodologies including indicators and benchmarks [2], or (b) following a Commission decision (ex officio or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel), has capabilities or an impact equivalent to point (a), having regard to the criteria in Annex XIII [2]. High impact capabilities are presumed where the cumulative training computation exceeds 10^25 floating point operations [2]. For the equivalence determination, Annex XIII says the Commission shall take into account: (a) the number of parameters; (b) the quality or size of the data set, e.g. measured through tokens; (c) the amount of training computation, or proxies such as estimated training cost, time or energy consumption; (d) input and output modalities and state-of-the-art thresholds for high-impact capabilities per modality; (e) benchmarks and evaluations of capabilities, including number of tasks without additional training, adaptability, level of autonomy and scalability, and tools access; (f) high impact on the internal market due to reach, presumed when made available to at least 10 000 registered business users established in the Union; and (g) the number of registered end-users [3]. Under Article 52(4), the Commission may designate a model as presenting systemic risks, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria [1]. Under Article 52(1), if the Commission becomes aware of an un-notified model presenting systemic risks, it may designate it [4]. The excerpts do not set out the detailed procedure beyond these points, and the delegated-act powers to amend thresholds and Annex XIII are noted in [1][2].

Under Article 53(1), providers of general-purpose AI models shall: (a) draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at minimum the Annex XI information, for provision upon request to the AI Office and national competent authorities [3]; (b) draw up, keep up-to-date and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model, enabling them to understand the model's capabilities and limitations, containing at minimum the Annex XII elements, without prejudice to intellectual property rights, confidential business information or trade secrets [3]; (c) put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including identifying and complying with reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [3]; and (d) draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, according to a template provided by the AI Office [2]. Providers must also cooperate as necessary with the Commission and national competent authorities [1]. Providers may rely on codes of practice under Article 56 to demonstrate compliance, until a harmonised standard is published, and those not adhering to an approved code or harmonised standard must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment [1]. Exception: points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1) do not apply to providers of models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, with weights, architecture and usage information publicly available; this exception does not apply to models with systemic risks [1]. Article 54 (authorised representatives) likewise does not apply to such open-source models unless they present systemic risks [4]. Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk have additional obligations under Article 55(1), including model evaluation with adversarial testing, assessing and mitigating systemic risks, reporting serious incidents, and ensuring cybersecurity [6]. The excerpts do not cover the full content of Annexes XI and XII, the Article 54 authorised representative mandate requirements beyond the points quoted, or the Article 56 codes of practice details.

Partly. Under Article 53(2), the obligations in Article 53(1)(a) and (b) (technical documentation and information/documentation for downstream AI system providers) do not apply to providers of models released under a free and open-source licence that allows access, usage, modification and distribution, and whose parameters (including weights), architecture information and usage information are made publicly available [1]. The exemption does not cover Article 53(1)(c), the copyright policy obligation, which the excerpts do not exempt [6]. Under Article 54(6), the obligation to appoint an authorised representative likewise does not apply to such open-source models [2]. Neither exemption applies to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk [1][2]. Systemic-risk models are subject to the additional Article 55(1) obligations (model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity) in addition to Articles 53 and 54 [4]. The excerpts do not state whether the open-source exemption affects any other obligations, such as those in Article 55 for systemic-risk models, beyond what is quoted. Under Article 53(4), providers may rely on codes of practice under Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1) obligations until a harmonised standard is published [1].

Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must comply with the obligations in Articles 53 and 54 plus, under Article 55(1), additional obligations: (a) perform model evaluation under standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including documented adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks [1]; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, that may stem from development, placing on the market, or use of the model [1]; (c) keep track of, document, and report without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities, relevant information on serious incidents and possible corrective measures [1]; and (d) ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure [1]. Article 55(2) allows them to rely on codes of practice under Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with Article 55(1) until a harmonised standard is published, with presumption of conformity from compliance with harmonised standards; those not adhering to an approved code or harmonised standard must show alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment [4]. Article 55(3) states that information obtained under this Article, including trade secrets, is subject to the confidentiality obligations in Article 78 [4]. The open-source exemptions in Article 53(2) and Article 54(6) do not apply to systemic-risk models [2][3]. A model is classified as systemic-risk under Article 51 where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, or where the Commission so decides [5]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed content of the Article 53 and 54 obligations themselves, nor the Article 56 codes of practice beyond the reference above.

Under Article 52(1), the provider must notify the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks after the Article 51(1)(a) requirement is met or it becomes known that it will be met [1]. The notification must include the information necessary to demonstrate that the requirement has been met [1]. This applies to the high-impact-capabilities condition in Article 51(1)(a), which is presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations under Article 51(2) [2]. The excerpts do not cover the separate case where a model is designated under Article 51(1)(b) or by the Commission under Article 52(4) [2][4].
unsupported_claims: The excerpts do not cover designation under Article 51(1)(b) or designation by the Commission under Article 52(4).

items.answer: Codes of practice are a voluntary route to demonstrating compliance for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers. The AI Office must encourage and facilitate their drawing up at Union level, and they should at least cover the obligations in Articles 53 and 55, including items such as keeping information up to date, the level of detail of training-content summaries, identifying systemic risks, and risk assessment and management measures [6]. Providers of GPAI models may rely on codes of practice to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1) obligations until a harmonised standard is published [5]. Providers of GPAI models with systemic risk may likewise rely on codes of practice under Article 55(1) for the same purpose until a harmonised standard is published [3]. Providers who do not adhere to an approved code, or do not comply with a harmonised standard, must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission [3][5]. The AI Office and the Board must monitor and evaluate whether codes achieve their objectives and publish their assessment of adequacy, and the Commission may approve a code by implementing act giving it general validity in the Union [2]. The AI Office may invite all GPAI providers to adhere, and for providers without systemic risk adherence may be limited to Article 53 obligations unless they declare interest in the full code [2]. Codes were to be ready by 2 May 2025; if not finalised by 2 August 2025, or deemed inadequate, the Commission may set common rules by implementing act [4]. The excerpts do not state the exact content of any specific finalised code or its legal status beyond these points.

Definition: an 'AI regulatory sandbox' is a controlled framework set up by a competent authority which offers providers or prospective providers of AI systems the possibility to develop, train, validate and test, where appropriate in real-world conditions, an innovative AI system, pursuant to a sandbox plan for a limited time under regulatory supervision [1]. Purpose: sandboxes provide a controlled environment that fosters innovation and facilitates development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before they are placed on the market or put into service, pursuant to a specific sandbox plan agreed between the providers or prospective providers and the competent authority; testing in real world conditions may be included under supervision [5]. Aims include improving legal certainty, supporting best-practice sharing, fostering innovation and competitiveness, contributing to evidence-based regulatory learning, and facilitating access to the Union market, particularly for SMEs including start-ups [2]. Who must set them up: Member States must ensure that their competent authorities establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, operational by 2 August 2026; this may be done jointly with other Member States' competent authorities, or by participating in an existing sandbox that provides an equivalent level of national coverage [3]. Additional regional, local or joint sandboxes may also be established [3]. The European Data Protection Supervisor may also establish a sandbox for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies [3]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed sandbox-plan content beyond the definition, or the full rules on participation, fees or exit reports beyond what is stated here; the sandbox-plan definition is given in Article 3(54) [1]. This is general information about the law, not legal advice.

Yes. Article 60(2) states that providers or prospective providers may conduct testing of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III in real world conditions at any time before the placing on the market or the putting into service of the AI system, on their own or in partnership with one or more deployers or prospective deployers [1]. This is subject to conditions: under Article 60(4), testing may only be conducted where all listed conditions are met, including that a real-world testing plan has been drawn up and submitted to the market surveillance authority in the Member State where testing will take place [4], and that authority has approved the testing and plan, with tacit approval after 30 days where national law provides for it, otherwise authorisation is required [4]. Other conditions include effective oversight by suitably qualified persons [3], informed consent of test subjects under Article 61 (with a law enforcement exception) [6], and that AI predictions, recommendations or decisions can be effectively reversed and disregarded [3]. Serious incidents must be reported to the market surveillance authority, and testing must be suspended or terminated where mitigation is not possible [2]. The provider is liable for any damage caused during testing [2]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed elements of the real-world testing plan, which are to be specified by the Commission through implementing acts [1]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

The excerpts describe several support measures. Member States must give SMEs and start-ups, with a registered office or branch in the Union, priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes if they meet eligibility and selection criteria, organise tailored awareness-raising and training, use or establish communication channels to answer queries, and facilitate their participation in standardisation [1]. Under Article 62(2), the specific interests and needs of SME providers and start-ups must be considered when setting conformity assessment fees under Article 43, with fees reduced proportionately to their size, market size and other relevant indicators [1]. The AI Office must provide standardised templates, maintain a single information platform, run awareness campaigns, and promote best practices in public procurement [2]. Under Article 58(2), sandboxes must allow free access for SMEs and start-ups, except for exceptional costs that national authorities may recover fairly and proportionately [5]; procedures must be simple and clear for SMEs with limited legal and administrative capacity [3]; and participation is limited to a period appropriate to the project, which may be extended [3]. Article 57(9)(e) states that sandbox objectives include facilitating and accelerating access to the Union market for AI systems, particularly those provided by SMEs and start-ups [4]. Article 1(2)(g) lists measures to support innovation with a particular focus on SMEs and start-ups as a purpose of the Regulation [6]. The excerpts do not cover the full details of how sandboxes are established or the specific conditions for fee reductions beyond the principle stated.

The Board is composed of one representative per Member State, and the European Data Protection Supervisor participates as an observer [1]. The AI Office attends the Board's meetings without taking part in the votes [1]. Other national and Union authorities, bodies or experts may be invited on a case-by-case basis where the issues discussed are relevant to them [1]. Each representative is designated by their Member State for three years, renewable once [1]. Member States must ensure their representatives have the relevant competences and powers, are a single contact point vis-à-vis the Board, and can facilitate consistency and coordination among national competent authorities [1] (Article 65(2)-(4)). The Board is chaired by one of the Member State representatives, and the AI Office provides its secretariat [2] (Article 65(8)). The representatives adopt the rules of procedure by a two-thirds majority [3] (Article 65(5)).

The scientific panel is a body of independent experts established by the Commission by implementing act to support enforcement activities under the AI Act [1]. Its members are experts selected by the Commission on the basis of up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in AI, who must have particular expertise, be independent from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models, and be able to act diligently, accurately and objectively [1]. Its main role is to advise and support the AI Office, in particular on enforcement for general-purpose AI models and systems (including alerting the AI Office to possible systemic risks, contributing to evaluation tools and benchmarks, and advising on classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk), supporting market surveillance authorities at their request, supporting cross-border market surveillance, and supporting the AI Office in Union safeguard procedures under Article 81 [5]. The panel may issue a duly reasoned qualified alert to the AI Office where it has reason to suspect that a general-purpose AI model poses a concrete identifiable risk at Union level or meets the conditions in Article 51 [6]. Member States may call upon panel experts to support their enforcement activities, and may be required to pay fees for this support [4]. Experts must act with impartiality and objectivity, keep information confidential, neither seek nor take instructions from anyone, and publish a declaration of interests [2]. The excerpts do not provide the panel's full composition, number of experts, or the detailed fee structure, which are left to the implementing act [1][4].

The excerpts only partly answer this. They refer to two kinds of national bodies: market surveillance authorities, which take measures on AI systems presenting a risk on their national market [5][6], and national public authorities or bodies that supervise or enforce Union law protecting fundamental rights in relation to high-risk AI systems in Annex III, which had to be identified and listed by 2 November 2024 [2]. Those bodies are referred to but not defined or named, and the excerpts do not say which specific authorities are designated in each Member State. They also do not cover the Commission's exclusive enforcement role for Chapter V general-purpose AI model obligations, beyond noting that the AI Office carries out those tasks [4]. The per-Member-State designations would need to be checked against the national lists and designation notices, which are not in the excerpts. This is not legal advice.

Under Article 72(1), providers must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system [1]. Under Article 72(2), the system must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data, which may be provided by deployers or collected from other sources, on the performance of the system throughout its lifetime, so the provider can evaluate continuous compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements; where relevant it must include analysis of interaction with other AI systems, and this obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law-enforcement authorities [1]. Under Article 72(3), the system must be based on a post-market monitoring plan that forms part of the technical documentation in Annex IV, and the Commission is to adopt an implementing act setting a template and list of plan elements by 2 February 2026 [1]. Under Article 72(4), for high-risk AI systems covered by Section A of Annex I where a monitoring system and plan already exist under that legislation, providers may choose to integrate the required elements into those existing systems and plans, provided they achieve an equivalent level of protection; this also applies to point 5 of Annex III systems placed on the market by financial institutions subject to Union financial services law on internal governance [2]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed template contents or other post-market obligations beyond these provisions, and Article 12(2)(b) notes that logging capabilities should facilitate post-market monitoring under Article 72 [5]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

The general deadline is not later than 15 days after the provider (or, where applicable, the deployer) becomes aware of the serious incident, with the report made immediately after a causal link, or its reasonable likelihood, has been established [1]. The period takes account of the severity of the incident [1]. Shorter deadlines apply in specific cases: in the event of a widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Article 3(49)(b), the report must be provided immediately and not later than two days after awareness [1]; in the event of the death of a person, the report must be provided immediately after a causal relationship is established or suspected, and not later than 10 days after awareness [2]. Where necessary for timely reporting, an initial incomplete report may be submitted, followed by a complete report [2]. For high-risk AI systems that are safety components of, or are, devices covered by Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746, notification is limited to incidents under Article 3(49)(c) and made to the chosen national competent authority [3]. Deployers that identify a serious incident must immediately inform first the provider, then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities [6]. The excerpts do not state the exact deadline for the deployer's own reporting beyond this immediate-notification duty, and this is information about the law, not legal advice.

Partly. Under Article 86(1) you have a right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision [1], but only if the decision is taken by the deployer on the basis of the output of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (excluding systems under point 2 of Annex III) [1], and it produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects you, in a way you consider to have an adverse impact on your health, safety or fundamental rights [1]. The right does not apply where exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law [1], and Article 86 applies only where the right is not otherwise provided for under Union law [1]. The excerpts do not cover the remaining Article 86 mechanics, the definition of the Annex III systems, or the Annex III point 2 exclusion, so whether a specific system falls within scope cannot be determined from them. Related duty: deployers of Annex III high-risk systems that make or assist decisions about natural persons must inform them that they are subject to such a system [6]. This is general information about the law, not legal advice.

Under Article 85, any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the Regulation may submit complaints to the relevant market surveillance authority, without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies [2]. Such complaints are taken into account for market surveillance activities under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and handled under the market surveillance authorities' dedicated procedures [2]. Where the complaint concerns a provider of a general-purpose AI model, downstream providers have the right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement; it must be duly reasoned and indicate at least the provider's point of contact, a description of the relevant facts and provisions, and the reason for the alleged infringement, and the AI Office may take monitoring actions under Article 89 [1]. The excerpts do not identify which specific national market surveillance authority is relevant in a given case, nor the detailed procedure for filing, so you would need to check the designated authority in your Member State.

For non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices in Article 5, administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [6] (Article 99(3)). Member States set the penalty rules, which must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive [6] (Article 99(1)). Separately, for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, the fine for non-compliance with Article 5 prohibitions is up to EUR 1 500 000 [3] (Article 100(2)); this Article 100 regime is not the general maximum for operators. The excerpts do not show the full list of Article 5 practices covered by the fines beyond those quoted, and this is information about the law, not legal advice.

Under Article 99(5), supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For SMEs, including start-ups, the applicable fine is the lower of the referenced percentage or amount, per Article 99(6) [1]. Separately, for providers of general-purpose AI models, Article 101(1)(b) allows the Commission to impose fines of up to 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where the provider intentionally or negligently supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request under Article 91 [2]. The excerpts do not state the SME rule for this Article 101 fine.

The excerpts do not contain the fine levels that apply to companies for non-compliance with high-risk AI system obligations. Article 80(4) and (7) [1] say providers are subject to fines 'in accordance with Article 99', but Article 99 is not among the excerpts, so its amounts are missing. The amounts that are included do not answer the question: Article 101 [2] sets fines of up to 3% of annual worldwide turnover or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, for providers of general-purpose AI models, and Article 100 [4] sets fines of up to EUR 750 000 for non-compliance by Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. Please provide Article 99 to answer this.

items.answer: Under Article 101(1) the Commission may impose on providers of general-purpose AI models fines not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher [1]. This applies when the Commission finds that the provider intentionally or negligently: (a) infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation; (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or information under Article 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information [1][4]; (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93 [1]; or (d) failed to give the Commission access to the general-purpose AI model, or model with systemic risk, for an evaluation under Article 92 [1][3]. In fixing the amount, regard is had to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, proportionality and appropriateness, and commitments made under Article 93(3) or in relevant codes of practice under Article 56 [1]. Before deciding, the Commission must communicate preliminary findings and give the provider an opportunity to be heard [1]. Fines must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive [1]. The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review such fines and may cancel, reduce or increase them [2]. The excerpts also refer to periodic penalty payments in Article 101(1) but do not give their amounts or conditions, which are not covered here.

Yes. Under Article 100(1), the European Data Protection Supervisor may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of the Regulation [2][4]. Article 100(2) sets fines of up to EUR 1 500 000 for non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibited AI practices, and Article 100(3) sets fines of up to EUR 750 000 for non-compliance of an AI system with other requirements or obligations under the Regulation [3]. Before deciding, the EDPS must give the institution, body, office or agency the opportunity to be heard, and decisions must rest only on elements the parties could comment on [3]. Fines collected go to the general budget of the Union and must not affect the effective operation of the fined entity [5]. Note that the excerpts do not show the full scope of Article 100 or the complete list of factors, and the Commission, not the EDPS, is the authority for fines on providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 101 [1][6].

Under Article 113, the Regulation enters into force on the twentieth day after its publication in the Official Journal [1]. It applies generally from 2 August 2026 [1]. However, Chapters I and II apply from 2 February 2025 [1]. Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII, and Article 78 apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101 [1]. Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations apply from 2 August 2027 [1]. The excerpts do not cover the application dates of other provisions not named in Article 113, nor the Article 113(3) carve-outs beyond what is cited in Article 111(1), which refers to Article 5 under Article 113(3)(a) [4]. Article 111(1) also states that AI systems that are components of large-scale IT systems in Annex X, placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027, must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030 [4].

items.answer: Yes, but with a transition period. Article 111(3) provides that providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 shall take the necessary steps to comply with the obligations laid down in the Regulation by 2 August 2027 [1]. The excerpts do not set out the content of every individual obligation, so they do not confirm whether any specific obligation applies earlier to these models, and they do not describe any exemptions beyond what Article 111(3) states.

Yes. Article 95(1) provides that the AI Office and the Member States shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application to AI systems, other than high-risk AI systems, of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 [1]. Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, and may cover one or more AI systems with similar intended purposes [2]. Article 95(2) states that the AI Office and Member States shall facilitate codes of conduct on voluntary application of specific requirements to all AI systems, including elements such as ethical guidelines for trustworthy AI, environmental sustainability, AI literacy, inclusive design, and preventing negative impact on vulnerable persons [3]. Article 95(4) requires that the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, be taken into account [2]. Article 112(7) requires the Commission to evaluate the impact and effectiveness of these voluntary codes of conduct by 2 August 2028 and every three years thereafter [5]. The excerpts do not contain further detail on the content, approval or enforcement of such codes.

Yes, in part. Article 87 provides that Directive (EU) 2019/1937 shall apply to the reporting of infringements of the Regulation and to the protection of persons reporting such infringements [1]. The excerpts do not set out the content of that protection itself, so the specific safeguards (e.g. channels, anti-retaliation measures) are not covered here and would need to be checked in Directive (EU) 2019/1937.

The excerpts describe the AI Office in part. Under Article 64(1), the Commission develops Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office, and under Article 64(2) Member States facilitate the tasks entrusted to it [6]. For general-purpose AI models, the AI Office may invite all providers of such models to adhere to codes of practice, and for providers not presenting systemic risks this may be limited to Article 53 obligations unless they declare explicitly their interest in the full code [5]. The AI Office, together with the Board, monitors and evaluates the achievement of code of practice objectives and assesses whether they cover the obligations in Articles 53 and 55, publishing its assessment of adequacy [5]. It also encourages and facilitates review and adaptation of codes of practice and assists in assessing available standards [5]. It takes the necessary steps to get codes of practice ready by 2 May 2025 [4]. The AI Office is supported by the scientific panel, which advises it on tasks such as classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk and supporting cross-border market surveillance and the Union safeguard procedure under Article 81 [1]. The Commission must evaluate by 2 August 2028 whether the AI Office has sufficient powers and competences [3]. The excerpts do not set out the AI Office's full range of powers, enforcement competences, or its role regarding AI systems beyond general-purpose AI models, so those aspects cannot be fully answered from them.

Yes, partly. Under Article 40(1), high-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models that conform to harmonised standards (or parts thereof) whose references are published in the Official Journal of the European Union under Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 are presumed to be in conformity with the requirements of Section 2 of Chapter III or, as applicable, the obligations in Chapter V, Sections 2 and 3, to the extent those standards cover those requirements or obligations [4]. The same presumption applies to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk under Article 55(2) [3] and to general-purpose AI model providers under Article 53(4) [2]. Article 32 gives a similar presumption for notified bodies meeting the Article 31 requirements, where applicable harmonised standards cover them [1]. Article 43(1) links the use of harmonised standards to the choice of conformity assessment procedure, with Annex VII required where standards do not exist, were not applied or were applied only in part [5]. Common specifications under Article 41(3) also carry a presumption of conformity to the extent they cover the requirements [6]. The excerpts do not state the full list of harmonised standards or their publication status, so whether a specific standard currently gives the presumption cannot be confirmed from them. Where providers do not comply with a harmonised standard, they must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission [2][3]. This is information about the law, not legal advice.

The excerpts describe a sequence depending on the finding. If a market surveillance authority, after evaluating an AI system under Article 79(2), finds it does not comply with the Regulation, it must without undue delay require the relevant operator to take appropriate corrective actions to bring the system into compliance, withdraw it from the market, or recall it, within a period the authority may prescribe and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period in relevant Union harmonisation legislation [4]. The authority must inform the relevant notified body, and Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies to these measures [4]. Where the system is compliant but still presents a risk to health, safety, fundamental rights or other public interest aspects, the authority, after consulting the relevant national public authority, must require the operator to take all appropriate measures so the system no longer presents that risk without undue delay, within a period it may prescribe [2]. The provider or other relevant operator must ensure corrective action across all affected AI systems it made available on the Union market [2]. The Member State must immediately inform the Commission and other Member States, and the Commission then consults and evaluates the national measures and decides whether they are justified [6]. Where an evaluation concerns a system classified as non-high-risk by the provider but found to be high-risk, the authority must require the provider to achieve compliance and take corrective action [3]. Relevant operators must cooperate with the authority [1]. The excerpts do not cover the detailed content of the Commission's further measures or the specifics of penalties.

Yes. Article 78(1) requires the Commission, market surveillance authorities, notified bodies and any other natural or legal person involved in applying the Regulation to respect the confidentiality of information and data obtained in carrying out their tasks, in accordance with Union or national law, so as to protect in particular intellectual property rights, trade secrets (including source code, subject to Article 5 of Directive (EU) 2016/943), the effective implementation of the Regulation, public and national security interests, criminal or administrative proceedings, and classified information [3]. Article 78(2) adds that the authorities involved must request only data strictly necessary for assessing risk and exercising their powers, put in place adequate and effective cybersecurity measures to protect the security and confidentiality of the information obtained, and delete the data as soon as it is no longer needed for its purpose, in accordance with applicable Union or national law [1]. Article 77(4) applies the Article 78 confidentiality obligations to information obtained by national public authorities or bodies under Article 77 [4], and Article 75(3) requires market surveillance authorities to safeguard the confidentiality of information obtained from the AI Office in line with Article 78 [5]. Article 78(3) further restricts disclosure of confidential information exchanged between national competent authorities or with the Commission where high-risk systems in Annex III points 1, 6 or 7 are used by law enforcement, border control, immigration or asylum authorities and disclosure would jeopardise public and national security, requiring prior consultation of the originating authority and the deployer [2]. The excerpts do not set out the full scope of the Article 78 obligations beyond these provisions. This is general information, not legal advice.

The excerpts do not contain the maximum fine for a personal data breach under the GDPR. They cover AI Act penalties only: Article 100 fines on Union institutions (up to EUR 1 500 000 for Article 5 non-compliance and up to EUR 750 000 for other non-compliance) [1], Article 99 fines for operators (up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, and up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1% for incorrect information) [6], and Article 10(5) references to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 without stating any GDPR fine amounts [2]. The GDPR's own penalty provisions are not included, so please consult Regulation (EU) 2016/679 directly.

The excerpts do not state what a notified body charges for certifying an AI system, and they contain no fee schedule or pricing rules. They cover notified body requirements (independence, competence, liability insurance under Article 31, and the duty to avoid unnecessary burdens and take account of provider size under Article 34(2) and Article 31(8)), but nothing on fees. Fees would need to be obtained directly from the notified body or the relevant national rules, which are outside these excerpts.

The excerpts cover only the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689): its scope, Annex III, sandboxes, the AI Office, the Board and market surveillance. They say nothing about US federal agencies or how AI is regulated in the United States, so the question cannot be answered from them.

The excerpts do not contain any information about the European Parliament vote count or the adoption procedure for the AI Act. They cover delegated act procedure (Article 97(6)), evaluation and review (Article 112), the Board's rules of procedure (Article 65) and an amendment to Regulation (EU) 2018/858 (Article 107), but nothing on how Parliament or Council voted when the Regulation was adopted.
